assets.topic: Keystone Habit vs. Spillover Change vs. Craving Signal
assets.visual_frame_description: A research laboratory outside Bethesda, Maryland. On a wall-sized monitor, brain-scan slices of Lisa Allen glow: a reddish cluster near the center of her brain and a bright band near her forehead. In the foreground, three labeled sorting columns hover over an evidence table, and the player drags glowing evidence chips into the correct category before the study team logs the session.
assets.player_mission: Sort each piece of evidence into the correct column: keystone habit, spillover change, or craving signal. Read each evidence chip drawn from Lisa Allen's case and classify all six correctly before the lab session timer runs out.
key_concepts: Lisa Allen started smoking and drinking when she was sixteen and struggled with obesity for most of her adult life.
By focusing on changing just one habit, smoking, Lisa taught herself how to reprogram the other routines in her life, a pattern researchers called a keystone habit.
Lisa's smoking was replaced by jogging, which in turn changed how she ate, worked, slept, saved money, and planned for the future.
Brain scans showed the regions near the center of Lisa's brain, associated with craving and hunger, still active when she saw food years after her habits changed.
Scans also showed new activity in the region near her forehead, believed to be where behavioral inhibition and self-discipline start, growing more pronounced with each visit.
As Lisa's habits changed, so had her brain: one set of neurological patterns, her old habits, had been overridden, though not erased, by new patterns.
The scientists concluded the Cairo trip itself did not cause the change; it was that Lisa had focused on changing just one habit first.
Companies such as Procter & Gamble, Starbucks, Alcoa, and Target have seized on the keystone-habit insight to influence how work gets done and how customers shop.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the keystone-habit mechanism: a single focused habit change can cascade into widespread change across other routines, as it did for Lisa Allen. The chapter grounds this in brain scans showing old craving patterns overridden rather than erased, and in the claim that individuals and whole organizations transform by focusing on one pattern.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Scientists studied Lisa Allen and more than two dozen other people who had remade their lives. Which column does each piece of evidence sort into?
assets.column_b_label: Spillover change (a routine that shifted because of the keystone)
assets.column_c_label: Craving signal (a neural urge that persisted)

rows.label: Lisa decided to quit smoking because she believed she had to, to survive her planned desert trek
After quitting cigarettes, Lisa started jogging, then running half-marathons
Lisa began saving money, sleeping better, and planning for the future
Brain scans showed regions near the center of her brain, tied to craving and hunger, still active when she saw food
New activity near her forehead, believed to be the seat of behavioral inhibition and self-discipline, strengthened each visit
By focusing on one pattern, Lisa taught herself to reprogram the other routines in her life

distractors: Old neural impulses were crowded out by new urges, so the original habit patterns vanished completely
The trip to Cairo itself caused the change, so keystone habits only apply to major life events
Only individuals, never companies or communities, can experience keystone-habit cascades
assets.explanation: Lisa's smoking was her keystone habit, the one pattern she focused on first, so evidence about her quitting decision sorts to column a. Jogging, saving, and scheduling were spillover changes that radiated outward once the keystone shifted, sorting to column b. The active craving regions and the strengthening prefrontal inhibition are neural signals the researchers observed, not habits themselves, so they sort to column c; the scans showed old patterns overridden, not erased.

assets.player_mission: Classify six everyday actions as deliberate decisions, automatic habits, or craving-driven urges. Use the chapter's distinction between behaviors chosen deliberately and behaviors that run without thinking to place each action in the right column.
key_concepts: William James wrote in 1892 that all our life, so far as it has definite form, is but a mass of habits.
Most of the choices people make each day feel like products of well-considered decision making, but they are actually habits.
A 2006 paper published by a Duke University researcher found that more than 40 percent of the actions people performed each day were not actual decisions, but habits.
Habits are defined as the choices we deliberately make at some point, and then stop thinking about but continue doing, often every day.
Each habit means relatively little on its own, but over time the meals we order and how often we exercise have enormous impacts on health, productivity, and financial security.
The morning routine, showering, checking email, grabbing a doughnut, and tying shoes in a fixed order, is presented as a chain of automatic behaviors.
The doctor told Lisa Allen that she was helping the researchers understand how a decision becomes an automatic behavior.
The military relies on endlessly rehearsed routines so that every command draws on behaviors practiced to the point of automation.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the automaticity of habits: behaviors that were once deliberate choices become routines we run without thinking. The chapter grounds this in William James's 1892 observation that life is a mass of habits and a 2006 Duke University finding that over 40 percent of daily actions are habits, not decisions.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: A 2006 Duke University study found that more than 40 percent of the actions people performed each day were not actual decisions but habits. Classify each everyday action.
assets.column_b_label: Automatic habit (done without thinking, no longer a choice)
assets.column_c_label: Craving-driven urge (a compulsive pull before the behavior)

rows.label: Choosing a graduate program after researching schools, finances, and career plans
Driving the same route to work while mentally planning the day
Tying the left shoe before the right shoe without noticing
Reaching for a cigarette in a dark hotel room before realizing the object is a pen

People run habits only when they are under stress or pressure
assets.explanation: The chapter argues that most choices feel like well-considered decisions but are actually habits: actions we once chose consciously and then stopped thinking about. A routine executed without deliberation, like the doughnut grab or the fixed shoe order, sorts to column b, while a researched life decision sorts to column a and a compulsive pull before the behavior, like reaching for a cigarette before recognizing a pen, sorts to column c.

assets.player_mission: Defeat the Keystone Cascade by first recognizing which single pattern triggered Lisa's transformation, then choosing the intervention that protects the keystone habit so the whole chain of routines stays transformed.
key_concepts: Lisa decided to quit smoking because she believed she had to in order to survive her planned desert trek.
The scientists concluded the Cairo trip itself did not cause the change; it was that Lisa had focused on changing just one habit at first.
By focusing on one pattern, a keystone habit, Lisa taught herself how to reprogram the other routines in her life.
Over the next six months Lisa replaced smoking with jogging, which changed how she ate, worked, slept, and saved.
She went on to run half-marathons, then a marathon, go back to school, buy a house, and get engaged.
Brain scans showed her old habit patterns overridden by new ones; the old impulses were crowded out by new urges.
Everyone in the NIH study had remade their lives in relatively short periods and had gone through a similar process of focused change.
Habit change, the chapter claims, radiates out from a single keystone to every part of a life.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the keystone-habit mechanism: transforming one central pattern triggers widespread change in other routines. The chapter grounds this in Lisa Allen's case, where focusing on quitting smoking rewired everything from her exercise to her finances, and in the claim that companies like Alcoa transform through a single keystone habit.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The keystone habit: focusing on one pattern first lets a person reprogram the other routines in life, because the change radiates outward from that single pattern.
assets.stage_1_observation: The scene opens in a Cairo hotel room at dawn. Lisa Allen, jet-lagged and heartbroken after her divorce, reaches for a cigarette in the dark and tries to light a pen. She has spent four months crying, binge eating, and feeling ashamed and angry. Later, riding in a taxi toward the Sphinx, she decides to come back to Egypt and trek the desert, giving herself one year to prepare. To survive, she concludes, she will have to quit smoking.
assets.stage_1_question: The scientists concluded that neither the Cairo trip, nor the divorce, nor the desert trek caused Lisa's transformation. What, in their view, actually touched off the chain of changes?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Lisa had focused on changing just one habit, smoking, at first; the keystone habit then carried the other routines in her life along with it.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Six months after quitting, Lisa still craves a cigarette, and her eating and savings routines are beginning to wobble. The researchers offer you three intervention plans. Choose the one most consistent with the keystone-habit mechanism described in the chapter.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Anchor the single keystone change, smoking replaced by jogging, so the cascade of sleep, saving, and scheduling improvements stays stable, rather than trying to fix every wobbling routine at once.

assets.topic: Coaching a Keystone Change
assets.visual_frame_description: A warm Portland coffee shop at dusk. Priya sits across from you, hands wrapped around a cold latte, a notebook of problems spread on the table. Behind her, a window fades into a montage of Lisa Allen jogging, then into a graphic of habit chains radiating from a single glowing link. The player's dialogue options appear as thought bubbles above the table.
assets.player_mission: Coach Priya through the conversation so she leaves with one clear keystone habit and a concrete replacement routine, steering her away from overwhelm, guesswork, and willpower-only promises.
key_concepts: Researchers found that everyone in the study had remade their lives in relatively short periods by focusing on changing just one habit at first.
By focusing on one pattern, a keystone habit, Lisa taught herself how to reprogram the other routines in her life.
Replacing smoking with jogging changed how Lisa ate, worked, slept, saved money, and planned for the future.
Habits are choices we deliberately make at some point and then stop thinking about but continue doing, often every day.
Brain scans showed Lisa's old habit patterns overridden by new ones as her habits changed.
The chapter claims transforming a habit is not necessarily easy or quick, but it is possible.
Lisa needed a goal to work toward, and her decision to trek the desert gave her a reason to make sacrifices.
The morning routine in the chapter shows that much of daily behavior runs automatically once choices become habits.
assets.theory_summary: This simulation tests the keystone-habit mechanism: transforming one central pattern triggers a cascade of change across other routines, as Lisa Allen's case demonstrates. The chapter's evidence, that study participants remade their lives by focusing on one pattern first, grounds the optimal coaching move.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: You are an old friend of Priya, a 32-year-old graphic designer in Portland. After a painful breakup, she has spent four months binge eating at night, drinking most evenings, sleeping poorly, and calling in sick at work. She asked you to meet her at a coffee shop to talk about getting her life back. Your goal is to help her see how to start, using what the chapter teaches about keystone habits and how a decision becomes an automatic behavior. The stakes are high: a single misstep in the conversation could send her back to resignation.
dialogue: Priya: I know I have to fix everything, my health, my savings, my job, my mood. I just don't know where to begin, and honestly the list makes me want to give up.
You: Start small. You don't fix a life in one weekend. What's the one thing that, if it changed, would make everything else feel easier?
Priya: Maybe quitting the evening drinking? But then I'd have nothing to unwind with, and I'd lie in bed thinking about him.
You: That's exactly the point. If drinking is the keystone, replacing it with something concrete, like a short run, might pull sleep, eating, and even your mornings along with it.
Priya: So I pick one habit, change it, and the rest just follows? That sounds too good to be true.
You: That's what the science suggests. People who remade their lives tended to focus on one pattern first, and the change radiated out to their other routines.
Priya: Okay. So which habit should it be?
choices: Let's build a ranked list of all five problems and fix them in order of importance, one week at a time.
Pick the one habit you believe will carry the others along, commit to replacing it with a concrete routine, and protect that single change first.
Ignore habits entirely. Tonight, just use sheer willpower to refuse the drink and see if you feel better tomorrow.
Start with your diet, since food controls your energy, and add the rest once your eating is under control.
assets.theoretical_principle: Keystone habit (focused change on one pattern reprograms other routines)
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 1 mirrors Lisa Allen's path: the chapter concludes the study's participants remade their lives by focusing on one keystone habit first, letting the change radiate to sleeping, eating, saving, and career. It also fits the definition of habits as choices we make and then stop thinking about, so Priya needs a concrete replacement routine, not a vague vow. Choice 0 overwhelms her with the same long list that drove her to resignation, choice 2 treats change as a one-night willpower contest even though the chapter shows habits persist automatically, and choice 3 picks a habit on a guess rather than on which pattern is actually central, which the chapter gives no basis for assuming.

assets.topic: Persuading the Data Skeptic
assets.visual_frame_description: A glass-walled conference room at 9 a.m., a whiteboard covered with a bar chart labeled daily actions: decisions vs. habits. Dana stands at the far end with her arms crossed; the director taps a pen. A faint supermarket aisle renders in the window, shoppers moving in repeated patterns, as the player's dialogue options float over the table.
assets.player_mission: Win the budget by persuading Dana with evidence, not insults: cite the chapter's research on automaticity and the corporate examples of habit-driven retail so the room approves the pilot.
key_concepts: A 2006 Duke University study found that more than 40 percent of the actions people performed each day were not actual decisions, but habits.
Most choices feel like products of well-considered decision making, but they are not; they are habits.
Firms such as Procter & Gamble, Starbucks, Alcoa, and Target have seized on habit insights to influence how work gets done and, without customers realizing it, the way people shop.
Habits are choices we consciously made at some point and then stopped thinking about but continue doing, often every day.
William James wrote in 1892 that all our life, so far as it has definite form, is but a mass of habits.
Over time, the meals we order, how often we exercise, and the way we organize our thoughts and work routines have enormous impacts on financial security and happiness.
The chapter says it is possible to rebuild these patterns in whichever way you choose by understanding how they happen.
Companies have used habit insights to influence employees' communication and the way people shop without customers realizing it.
assets.theory_summary: This simulation tests the automaticity of habits: behaviors we once chose continue running without deliberation, which is why companies engineer for routine rather than fresh choice. The chapter grounds this in the 2006 Duke finding that over 40 percent of daily actions are habits and in the claim that P&G, Starbucks, Alcoa, and Target use habit insights to influence how customers shop.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: You are a strategy analyst at a mid-sized retailer, in a Monday-morning planning meeting. Dana, the head of merchandising, insists every purchase is a rational, moment-by-moment decision, so she sees no point in studying customer routines. Your director has asked you to convince the team that habits shape buying, because the company wants to design promotions around routine behavior. The stakes: if you convince the room, you get budget for a habit-focused pilot; if you fail, the project is shelved.
dialogue: Dana: Customers are rational. They look at price, features, and reviews, and they decide. I don't see what habits have to do with buying.
You: Some decisions are deliberate, but a lot of what we do all day isn't a decision at all. There's research showing most of our daily actions are habits.
Dana: Sure, for brushing teeth. Not for opening a wallet. People think before they spend.
You: Companies like Procter & Gamble and Target built growth on understanding that shoppers follow routines without realizing it.
Dana: So you want me to believe shoppers are sleepwalking?
You: Not sleepwalking, repeating. They chose a routine once, then stopped thinking about it. That's what a habit is.
choices: A 2006 Duke University study found that more than 40 percent of the actions people perform each day aren't actual decisions, but habits. If shopping is mostly routine, we should design for the routine.
If customers were rational, nobody would buy the same brand twice, so your model is obviously wrong.
We don't need the science. Let's just offer a discount to first-time buyers and see what happens.
You're right that spending is different. Let's drop the whole habit idea and focus on price matching.
assets.theoretical_principle: Automaticity of habit (a formerly chosen behavior runs without deliberation, so much of daily action is not decision-making)
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 grounds the pitch in the chapter's evidence, the 2006 Duke finding that more than 40 percent of daily actions are habits rather than decisions, and connects it to the chapter's claim that firms like P&G and Target influence the way people shop, giving Dana a specific, falsifiable fact instead of an insult. Choice 1 attacks her with a false dichotomy, since rationality does not require never repeating a purchase, which only makes her defensive; choice 2 abandons the analysis and gambles on a discount, missing the argument's point; choice 3 surrenders entirely and shelves the pilot.

chapters.title: 1. The Habit Loop: How Habits Work

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Cue, Routine, Reward: Components of the Habit Loop
assets.visual_frame_description: A split-screen laboratory collage. On the left, a rat sprints through a T-shaped maze toward a piece of chocolate as a partition lifts with a loud click. On the right, an elderly Eugene sits at a table with sixteen small objects glued to cardboard rectangles, flipping one over to reveal a sticker. Thin yellow arrows loop between labeled boxes labeled 'cue,' 'routine,' and 'reward.'
assets.player_mission: Sort each piece of evidence into the correct part of the habit loop: cue, routine, or reward. Identify which component the question highlights and confirm you can parse any behavior into the loop's three stages.
key_concepts: The habit loop is a three-step cycle: a cue triggers the brain to go into automatic mode, a routine follows, and a reward tells the brain whether the loop is worth remembering.
In the MIT T-maze experiments, the loud click of the partition was the cue that told each rat which habit to use.
The routine of a habit can be physical, mental, or emotional.
The reward helps the brain figure out if the particular loop is worth remembering for the future.
Over time the cue and reward become intertwined until a powerful sense of anticipation and craving emerges.
Eugene was exposed to a cue (the same pairings of objects), performed a routine (choosing and flipping a card), and received a reward (the satisfaction of finding a 'correct' sticker).
Brain activity spikes at the start of a habit, when the brain searches for a cue, and again at the end, when the reward appears.
A cue can be a visual trigger, a place, a time of day, an emotion, a sequence of thoughts, or the company of particular people.
Once a habit emerges, the brain stops fully participating in decision making and the pattern unfolds automatically.
When the habit loop is intact, the behavior becomes automatic; Eugene's morning walk ran because consistent trees and mailboxes served as cues.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the three-part habit loop: a cue triggers an automatic routine that ends in a reward, which determines whether the brain remembers the loop. The book's evidence from the MIT rat mazes and Squire's card experiments with Eugene shows that every habit can be decomposed into these components.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: In the MIT rat-maze experiment, the loud 'click' of the partition before the rat runs tells the animal which pattern to use. Which component of the habit loop does the click represent?

rows.label: The loud click of the partition opening before the rat starts running
The rat sprinting straight to the chocolate after a week of practice
The chocolate the rat eats at the end of the maze
Eugene being offered the same pair of cardboard objects in Squire's test
Eugene choosing one object and turning it over to check for a sticker

assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The standardized architecture, greeting, and visual triggers, such as the arches and the play area, are the consistent cues that trigger the eating routine, and the fries' engineered fast delivery of salt and grease is the immediate reward that lights up the pleasure centers and locks in the pattern. The routine is the eating itself, and the loop tightens with each visit.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Six months later the McDonald's near the Gomezes closes for remodeling, and the family stops going. Your colleague argues this proves the habit is weak and will not return. How should you correct her, using the chapter?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The closing shows that habits are delicate, even small shifts in cues can end a pattern, which is exactly why learning to observe cues and rewards gives us control. But Graybiel's work shows the neural pattern never disappears: if the restaurant reopens or a similar set of cues returns, the loop can reemerge, so the parents should deliberately build a new routine, such as cooking dinner at home, that overpowers the old one rather than assume the habit is gone.

assets.topic: Explaining Eugene's Automatic Behaviors

Eugene's basal ganglia escaped injury from the viral encephalitis and stored his habits.
Eugene chose the correct object 85 percent of the time after twenty-eight days and 95 percent after thirty-six days.

The habit loop is a cue, a routine, and a reward that becomes more automatic over time.
The consistent trees and mailboxes on Eugene's walking route served as cues that guided him home.
Habits, as much as memory and reason, are at the root of how we behave.
Habits can emerge outside our consciousness or can be deliberately designed.
Chunking lets the basal ganglia run an automatic routine while conscious brain regions go quiet.
Without the basal ganglia, people become mentally paralyzed and lose access to hundreds of daily habits.

Eugene's intact basal ganglia ran cue-routine-reward loops even though his medial temporal lobe was destroyed, which is why he could perform complex automatic behaviors he could never remember.

assets.scenario_setup: You are a graduate researcher in Larry Squire's lab at UCSD. A visiting psychology professor has just watched Eugene find the bathroom, walk home alone, and flip 'correct' cards, and she is baffled, because Eugene cannot draw a map of his own house. She corners you in the hallway and asks how any of this is possible. Your credibility in the lab and the accuracy of the published account depend on explaining the neuroscience clearly.
dialogue: Visiting professor: 'He can't tell me where his kitchen is, yet he just walked in there and got a jar of nuts. What on earth is going on in his brain?'
You: 'The kitchen map is gone along with his medial temporal lobe, but the route to the nuts was never stored there. That trip is a habit.'
Visiting professor: 'A habit? He lost the ability to form new memories months ago. How does a man with no memory form anything new?'
You: 'That is exactly the surprise. Squire's card test proved it: Eugene picked the correct object 95 percent of the time after 36 days and still could not recall any of it.'
Visiting professor: 'So what is storing it? Some kind of reflex?'

You: 'Not a reflex, a habit loop. The same pairings are the cue, choosing and flipping the card is the routine, and the correct sticker is the reward. The encephalitis spared his basal ganglia, and that is where the loop is encoded.'
Visiting professor: 'And the walking home, the bathroom visits?'
You: 'Same machinery. The trees and mailboxes along his route are consistent cues; his basal ganglia runs the walking chunk while his conscious memory stays silent.'
choices: Explain that Eugene runs cue-routine-reward loops stored in his intact basal ganglia, while his destroyed medial temporal lobe wiped out conscious memory, which is exactly what Squire's experiments demonstrated.
Suggest that Eugene must secretly remember more than he admits and that the tests are unreliable.
Tell her the behavior is a lucky coincidence and that Squire has not been able to replicate it.
Say the walking and card choices are reflexes like the startle response, with no learning involved.
assets.theoretical_principle: The habit loop (cue-routine-reward) and the basal ganglia's role in chunking and storing habits independently of conscious memory.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 works because it matches the book's account: Squire proved it is possible to learn and make unconscious choices without remembering anything about the lesson, with habits stored in the basal ganglia. Choice 1 misreads the data, since Eugene genuinely has no conscious memory of the objects. Choice 2 contradicts the replicated card experiment (85 percent at day 28, 95 percent at day 36). Choice 3 confuses habit with reflex: habits are learned, deliberate, context-dependent loops, not hardwired startle responses.

assets.topic: Retraining a 3 p.m. Snacking Loop
assets.visual_frame_description: A bright break room in a Chicago accounting firm. Priya, thirty-eight, in a cardigan, leans on a counter beside a communal cookie jar, looking frustrated. You sit across from her with a notepad, and a small whiteboard on the wall shows a circle drawn in three parts labeled 'cue,' 'routine,' and 'reward.'
assets.player_mission: Coach Priya through the habit loop so she can stop her 3 p.m. cookie habit for good. Choose the advice that keeps the cue and reward intact while replacing the routine, rather than strategies the book shows are ineffective.
key_concepts: Habits emerge because the brain is constantly looking for ways to save effort.
Unless you deliberately fight a habit, unless you find new routines, the pattern will unfold automatically.
The cue and reward become intertwined until a powerful sense of anticipation and craving emerges.
Once you break a habit into its components, you can fiddle with the gears.
Beverly inserted new cues, such as not keeping bacon in the fridge, to short-circuit Eugene's bad patterns.
When Beverly put a salad next to Eugene's chair, the meal became a habit and he stopped searching the kitchen for treats.
The brain can't tell the difference between bad and good habits.
Habits never really disappear; they are encoded into the structures of the brain.
If we learn to create new neurological routines that overpower old behaviors, we can force bad tendencies into the background.
Once someone creates a new pattern, it becomes as automatic as any other habit.

The chapter's evidence from Beverly's interventions with Eugene shows that changing the middle of the loop while preserving its ends allows a new pattern to take root and the old one to fade into the background.

assets.scenario_setup: You are a workplace wellness coach meeting Priya, a thirty-eight-year-old accountant, in the break room of her firm's Chicago office. Priya is frustrated: every afternoon around 3 p.m., when her energy dips, she eats several cookies from the communal jar by the coffee machine and then feels guilty. She has tried just saying no for months and always caves, and she wants a plan that will actually stick. If you send her off with pure willpower advice she will fail and lose trust in the program.
dialogue: Priya: 'I've tried to quit the cookies a hundred times. By 3 p.m. my brain just seems to switch off and my hand is in the jar.'
You: 'That's not a lack of willpower, it's a habit loop. Let's find the cue that starts it.'
Priya: 'The cue? It's just being tired and bored at my desk.'
You: 'Okay, so time of day and that slump. And what does eating the cookies give you, beyond sugar?'
Priya: 'Honestly? A minute away from my screen. A little pleasure. A reset.'
You: 'Good. So we keep that reward, keep the 3 p.m. cue, and change only the routine.'
Priya: 'Wait, you're not going to tell me to empty the jar?'
You: 'That works only as long as the jar stays empty. A habit doesn't erase itself; the loop just needs a new routine to discharge into.'
choices: Recommend keeping the 3 p.m. cue and the reset-and-pleasure reward, but swap the cookie routine for a short walk or a stretching break she genuinely enjoys.
Tell her to empty the cookie jar and simply rely on discipline until the craving fades.
Suggest she ignore the 3 p.m. feeling entirely and push through her work without any break.
Advise her to shame herself with a sticky note listing calories so guilt stops her.
assets.theoretical_principle: Habit-loop retraining: keep the cue and reward, replace the routine. The chapter claims that unless you deliberately find new routines the old pattern unfolds automatically, and that inserting new routines forces bad tendencies into the background, as Beverly did by removing bacon and adding a salad for Eugene.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 fits the book's model: the loop's energy gets a new routine while the cue and reward stay intact, so the brain keeps its payoff without the unwanted behavior. Choice 1 relies on willpower and leaves the cue-reward pair intact, so the loop reasserts itself, and the brain cannot tell good from bad habits. Choice 2 fights the loop with suppression, and since habits emerge without permission the routine unfolds anyway. Choice 3 adds guilt, which the chapter never supports as a mechanism; emotional payoffs such as pride, not shame, are the rewards the book identifies as anchors.

key_concepts: A habit loop consists of a cue, a routine, and a reward.
Hopkins's first rule was to find a simple and obvious cue.
Hopkins's second rule was to clearly define the rewards.
Tooth film was a universal cue that almost anyone could feel by running a tongue across the teeth.
Pepsodent's formula contained citric acid, mint oil, and other irritants that created a cool, tingling sensation on the tongue and gums.
Customers who forgot to brush said they missed the tingling sensation, and their mouths did not feel clean without it.
A decade after the first Pepsodent campaign, toothbrushing had become a daily ritual for more than half of Americans.
Before Pepsodent appeared, only 7 percent of Americans had a tube of toothpaste in their medicine chests; a decade later the number reached 65 percent.
The sight of a pack of cigarettes is enough for a smoker's brain to crave a nicotine rush.
Once a craving exists, the habit loop spins automatically, even in the face of strong disincentives.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the habit loop: a cue triggers a routine that delivers a reward, and the loop only becomes automatic when the brain begins to crave the reward. The chapter argues that Hopkins succeeded not by selling clean teeth but by selling a sensation customers learned to crave.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Each row is an element of the toothbrushing habit Claude Hopkins built with Pepsodent. Classify each element as a cue, a routine, or a reward, then identify which element Hopkins was really selling.

Brushing your teeth with Pepsodent every morning
The cool tingling sensation on the tongue and gums
A yellow spiral flashing on a monitor screen
Touching the lever when a shape appears

assets.topic: Hopkins's Three Rules: The Hidden Third Element
assets.visual_frame_description: An old advertising office appears on screen with three filing cabinets labeled 'Simple Cue,' 'Clear Reward,' and 'Craving.' Claude Hopkins's desk is piled with dental textbooks, and a brass plaque reads 'Laws of Scientific Advertising.' Evidence cards drift past, each showing a fragment of the Pepsodent or Febreze story.
assets.player_mission: Classify each element of the Pepsodent and Febreze stories into the rule it illustrates, then identify which column represents the hidden third element that actually powered both campaigns.
key_concepts: Hopkins's two rules were to find a simple, obvious cue and to clearly define the reward.
The book argues these two rules are not enough: a third element, craving, must be created.
Earlier toothpastes such as Sanitol and S.S. White had already advertised film removal and beautiful teeth without success.
Pepsodent succeeded because its citric acid and mint oils produced a tingling sensation people began to crave.
Dozens of ad men used the same language as Pepsodent for years, yet none of their products took off.
Hopkins himself relied on the craving principle without knowing it existed.
A craving is what makes cues and rewards work, because it powers the habit loop.
Once customers craved the tingling, brushing became automatic and their mouths felt unclean without it.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the distinction between Hopkins's two explicit rules and the hidden third element the book argues is decisive: craving. Duhigg contends that a cue and a reward alone do not sustain a habit; the loop only spins when the brain anticipates and craves the reward.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Hopkins boasted of two rules for building new habits, but a third, hidden element was the real engine of his success. Classify each element of the Pepsodent and Febreze stories into the rule it illustrates, then identify the hidden third element.
assets.column_c_label: Cultivate a craving (the hidden third element)

rows.label: The film you can feel by running your tongue across your teeth
Beautiful, white Pepsodent smiles promised in the ads
The cool tingling customers said they missed when they forgot to brush
Febreze repositioned as the nice smell that ends a cleaning routine
An evening of guilt-free television after a workout
Lacing up running shoes as soon as you get home from work

distractors: Hopkins's two published rules are sufficient to create a lasting new habit.
A craving is a purely physiological hunger and cannot be created by advertising.
The cue and the reward must be unrelated to each other for the loop to form.
assets.explanation: The chapter's central argument is that Hopkins's two published rules were incomplete: cues and rewards work only because they produce a craving, the third element that drives the loop. Earlier toothpastes had already used the same cue and reward, but Pepsodent added a tingling sensation customers came to crave, and a craving for a nice smell at the end of cleaning is what finally made Febreze sell.

The Scottsdale mother who sprayed Febreze after every room and emptied a bottle every two weeks

assets.topic: Schultz's Monkey: The Stages of Habit Formation
assets.visual_frame_description: A dimly lit Cambridge laboratory appears on screen, with a small macaque named Julio sitting in a chair facing a monitor. assets.player_mission: Classify each observation from Wolfram Schultz's monkey experiments into the stage of habit formation it reflects, then identify the stage that explains why established habits resist distraction.
key_concepts: Schultz monitored monkeys with electrodes as they learned to touch a lever when shapes appeared on a screen.
Early on, the 'I got a reward!' brain pattern fired only after the blackberry juice arrived.
As the habit strengthened, that pattern began firing at the sight of the shapes, before the juice arrived.
When juice was withheld, late, or watered down, Julio grew angry, made unhappy noises, and showed a craving pattern.
Monkeys with established habits ignored food and the open door, staying to press the lever again and again.
Monkeys without a strong habit left for the distractions and never looked back.
Anticipation and craving, once created, hold sway over behavior even in the face of strong disincentives.
The craving emerges so gradually that people are often blind to its influence.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests Schultz's finding that habit formation shifts the reward signal earlier, to the cue, creating anticipation and then craving. Once craving is established, the animal acts automatically and ignores competing incentives, the same way a gambler keeps playing slots after losing.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Schultz's experiments with Julio revealed how a rewarded action becomes a habit. Classify each observation into the stage of the process it reflects, then identify the stage that explains why established habits resist distraction.

rows.label: Julio squirming in the chair and ignoring the monitor before the first dose of juice
The 'I got a reward!' pattern firing the instant the shape appears, before any juice
Julio staying glued to the screen despite food in the corner and the door open to the outdoors
Unhappy noises and a desire-and-frustration pattern when the juice is delayed or diluted
Julio touching the lever whenever a yellow spiral or blue line flashes

Anticipation and craving, not the reward itself, came to drive the behavior.

assets.topic: Building a Morning Running Habit from Cue, Reward, and Craving
assets.visual_frame_description: A quiet apartment at dawn shows Maya, a 34-year-old accountant, in pajamas looking at running shoes laid out on the floor beside her bed. A breakfast table, a smoothie glass, and a workout-log app float nearby as decision prompts, with a calendar marking each successful morning run.
assets.player_mission: Coach Maya through the chapter's formula for creating an exercise habit: select a simple cue and a clear reward, then take the decisive step that makes the routine automatic. Defeat the temptation to rely on sheer willpower.
key_concepts: Habitual exercisers in the New Mexico State study had started almost on a whim but continued because of a reward they came to crave.
92 percent of one group said they exercised because it made them feel good.
67 percent of another group said exercise gave them a sense of accomplishment from tracking their performance.
A good cue is simple, like running as soon as you get home from work or lacing up sneakers before breakfast.
A clear reward might be a beer, an evening of guilt-free television, or recording your miles.
Countless studies show a cue and a reward on their own are not enough for a habit to last.
The cue must trigger not only the routine but also a craving for the reward to come.
Once the brain expects the reward, lacing up the running shoes becomes automatic.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the chapter's claim that cue and reward alone do not create a lasting habit; the decisive ingredient is craving the reward before the routine happens. The research showed successful exercisers had come to crave either the feel-good endorphins or a sense of accomplishment.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is the personal formula for building a new habit: choose a simple cue, define a clear reward, and then cultivate the craving for that reward so the loop runs automatically.
assets.stage_1_observation: Maya is a 34-year-old accountant who wants to start running every morning before work. She tells you her past attempts always began with enthusiasm and ended within three weeks. She has a roommate who works nights, so mornings are quiet. The chapter's description of the New Mexico State study shows that habitual exercisers typically chose a simple cue and a clear reward.
assets.stage_1_question: Which cue-and-reward pair best matches what the chapter's research found helps people stick with exercise?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: A simple, specific cue such as lacing up her sneakers before breakfast or leaving running clothes next to her bed, paired with a clear reward such as a smoothie, guilt-free television, or recording her miles for a sense of accomplishment.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Maya has now run every day for two weeks with her chosen cue and reward, but she asks why the routine still feels effortful and worries she will quit. Based on the chapter's argument that cue and reward alone are not enough, what is the decisive next step?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: She must allow herself to anticipate the reward, thinking about the endorphin rush or the satisfaction of recording her miles, so her brain learns to crave it; only then does lacing up her shoes become automatic.

assets.topic: The Pepsodent Secret: Hopkins Was Selling a Sensation
assets.visual_frame_description: A vintage advertising archive shows stacks of faded magazine pages: Dr. Sheffield's Crème Dentifrice promising to clean the dirty layer, Sanitol promising to restore original whiteness, and S.S. White praising beautiful, satin smooth teeth. Over them looms a giant Pepsodent tube with a minty blue mist curling around a pair of open lips.
assets.player_mission: Solve the mystery of why Pepsodent triumphed over nearly identical campaigns, then recommend how competitors should respond. Defeat the assumption that the advertised cue and reward were the real cause.
key_concepts: Sanitol, S.S. White, and Dr. Sheffield had used film-and-beauty appeals before Pepsodent without success.
Pepsodent's patent listed citric acid, mint oil, and other chemicals that irritate the tongue and gums.
Customers who forgot to brush said they missed the cool, tingling sensation in their mouths.
Hopkins boasted that he found a cue and reward, but the true driver was the craving for the tingle.
Within a few decades, almost every toothpaste contained chemicals that caused gums to tingle.
Brand manager Tracy Sinclair said the tingling just convinces people the product is doing the job.
Pepsodent demand exploded in the third week after the campaign launched.
By 1930 Pepsodent was sold in China, South Africa, Brazil, Germany, and almost anywhere else Hopkins could buy ads.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the chapter's claim that Hopkins was not selling clean teeth but a sensation, and that craving, not the advertised cue and reward, powered the habit. Competing companies could only copy the tingle, and today almost all toothpastes still add tingling or foaming agents solely to signal that the product is working.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is that Pepsodent's success did not come from its advertised cue and reward, which rival pastes had already used, but from an unadvertised ingredient that manufactured a craving: the tingling sensation.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are advising a historian writing about Claude Hopkins. He shows you advertisements that predate Pepsodent: Dr. Sheffield's Crème Dentifrice urged people to clean that dirty layer, Sanitol promised to restore original whiteness by removing film, and S.S. White sold beautiful, satin smooth teeth. All used tooth film as a cue and beauty as a reward, and all failed. Then Hopkins launched Pepsodent with nearly identical appeals, and demand exploded within three weeks.
assets.stage_1_question: Why did Pepsodent succeed where the identical appeals of Sanitol, S.S. White, and Dr. Sheffield had failed?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Pepsodent's formula contained citric acid, mint oil, and other irritants that created a cool, tingling sensation on the tongue and gums, a sensation customers came to crave so that their mouths did not feel clean without it.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Competitors have discovered Pepsodent's secret and ask you to recommend a response. Option A: copy the appeal to film and beauty even more aggressively. Option B: add tingle-producing chemicals to their own formulas so their pastes produce the same cool sensation. Option C: advertise that Pepsodent's tingling is unnecessary.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Option B: imitate the sensation, which is what the book says rivals actually did, so that within a few decades almost every toothpaste contained oils and chemicals that made gums tingle.

assets.topic: Weight-Loss Success: The Craving-Driven Diet

Charts track breakfast habits cued by the clock, a bikini hanging in a closet, and a bathroom scale glowing with pride, while a plate of late-night snacks tempts a dieter at the edge of the scene.
assets.player_mission: Determine why daily breakfast functions as a habit cue for successful dieters, then choose the strategy that matches the registry research when a dieter faces temptation. Defeat the belief that discipline alone keeps weight off.
key_concepts: The National Weight Control Registry involves more than six thousand people who each lost more than thirty pounds.
78 percent of successful dieters ate breakfast every morning.
The breakfast habit was cued by a time of day.
Successful dieters envisioned a specific reward they carefully chose and really wanted.
Examples of chosen rewards include a bikini they wanted to wear and the sense of pride from stepping on the scale.
Dieters focused on the craving for that reward when temptations arose.
The craving for the reward crowded out the temptation to drop the diet.
Cultivating the craving turned it into a mild obsession that drove the habit loop.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the chapter's claim that the most successful dieters paired a time-of-day cue with a carefully chosen, deeply wanted reward, then cultivated the craving for it until it dominated temptation. The craving, the book says, is what drives the habit loop.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept is how data on successful dieters reveals the craving-driven habit loop: a time-of-day cue, a chosen self-reward, and a cultivated craving that crowds out temptation.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are a behavioral researcher reviewing data from the National Weight Control Registry, a project involving more than six thousand people who have each lost more than thirty pounds. You are looking for the habits that separated people who kept the weight off from those who relapsed. The data shows that 78 percent of successful dieters ate breakfast every morning.
assets.stage_1_question: In the chapter's framework, what role does eating breakfast each morning play for these dieters?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: It is a routine cued by a specific trigger, the time of day, providing the simple, reliable cue the habit loop requires.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The successful dieters did more than eat breakfast. A dieter tells you she is about to cave to a late-night snack and asks what the registry research suggests she should do. You must choose the strategy that matches the book's findings.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Direct her attention to the specific reward she has chosen, such as the bikini she wants to wear or the pride she feels stepping on the scale, and let her crave it; the craving for that reward crowds out the temptation to break the diet.

assets.topic: Designing a Running Habit with Cue, Reward, and Craving
assets.visual_frame_description: Two friends sit at a corner café table on a rainy Saturday morning, one cradling a coffee cup with frustration, the other leaning in with a notebook. A running-track diagram and a list titled 'Cue, Reward, Craving' are sketched on a napkin between them, while rain streaks the window behind.
assets.player_mission: Guide Priya's advice to Maya as she designs a lasting running habit. Choose the response that applies the chapter's formula for building an automatic routine.
key_concepts: A good cue is simple and specific, such as leaving running clothes next to the bed.
A clear reward, like a smoothie or an evening of guilt-free television, closes the loop.
Cue and reward alone are not enough for a new habit to last.
The cue must also trigger a craving for the reward to come.
92 percent of one group of habitual exercisers craved the feel-good feeling of working out.
67 percent of another group craved a sense of accomplishment from tracking their performance.
Anticipating the reward helps the habit become automatic.
Once the brain expects the reward, lacing up the shoes becomes nearly effortless.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the craving-driven habit loop described in the chapter: a cue and a reward are necessary but insufficient until the brain anticipates and craves the reward. The chapter's exercise research shows habitual exercisers continued because they had come to crave the endorphins or the sense of accomplishment.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: Maya, 34, has told her friend Priya she wants to build a running habit and has failed four times. Priya has just read The Power of Habit and is helping Maya design her routine over coffee. The goal is to make running automatic; the stakes are Maya's self-confidence if she fails again.
dialogue: Maya: 'I always plan to run in the morning, but by 7 a.m. I've already talked myself out of it. How do people actually stick with this?'
Priya: 'What does a successful run feel like for you? What's the moment that makes it worth it?'
Maya: 'Honestly, the best part is after, I feel clear-headed all morning. And I love that I can log another run in my app.'
Priya: 'Good. Now, what is a simple, concrete thing that will always happen right before you run?'
Maya: 'I always wake up, and my running clothes are next to my bed. If I put them on first thing, I can't argue with myself.'
Priya: 'So your cue is the clothes by the bed. Now pick one reward, the clear-headed feeling or logging the run, and here's the trick: let yourself look forward to it.'
Maya: 'Look forward to it? I thought the whole point was discipline.'
Priya: 'That's the part people miss. The habit only becomes automatic once your brain starts craving that reward before you even lace up.'
choices: Stop overthinking it and tell her to use sheer willpower and wake up earlier.
Tell her to put on her shoes and run, and never mind the reward, because repetition is all that matters.
Confirm the specific cue and the clear reward, then have her practice anticipating that reward until she craves it.
Advise her to run at different times each day so the routine never gets boring.
assets.theoretical_principle: Hopkins's two rules, find a simple cue and define a clear reward, plus the hidden third element the chapter emphasizes: cultivating a craving for the reward.
assets.psychological_breakdown: The optimal choice matches the chapter's formula: a simple cue such as clothes by the bed, a clear reward such as the clear-headed feeling or logging the run, and, critically, anticipating the reward so the brain comes to crave it, which turns the routine into an automatic habit. Sheer willpower fails because it does not create craving, repetition without a reward does not last, and varying the cue removes the stable trigger the loop needs.

assets.topic: Repositioning an Air Freshener for Craving
assets.visual_frame_description: Two people sit in a bright café, one scrolling a phone showing a flat sales chart labeled 'FreshFinish,' the other sketching a room where a woman sprays a freshly made bed. A small bottle with the old tagline 'Eliminates bad odors' sits on the table between them.
assets.player_mission: Advise Ethan through the marketing dilemma by applying the Febreze lesson. Choose the response that converts a failing odor-elimination product into a craving-driven habit.
key_concepts: People become desensitized to smells they live with, so bad odors are not an effective cue.
Febreze's first campaign failed because the cue was invisible to the people who needed it most.
The relaunch made Febreze the reward that ends a cleaning routine.
The tagline changed from 'Gets bad smells out of fabrics' to 'Cleans life's smells.'
No one craves scentlessness, but many people crave a nice smell after thirty minutes of cleaning.
Sales doubled within two months of the 1998 relaunch.
Customers spent more than $230 million on Febreze within a year of the relaunch.
The craving for the finish, not the science of odor removal, drove the habit.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests Duhigg's account of why Febreze failed and succeeded: a cue people cannot perceive cannot trigger a habit, and a reward placed at the end of an existing routine can generate craving. After the repositioning, Febreze sales doubled within two months and exceeded $230 million within a year.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: Ethan has launched FreshFinish, a home fragrance spray, in two test cities and sales are flat. He meets Priya, a marketing consultant who has studied the Febreze story, at a café. Ethan's ads promise to eliminate bad odors; customers buy once and never repurchase. The stakes are the survival of Ethan's startup.
dialogue: Ethan: 'The science works, this spray really does kill odors. But nobody buys it twice. My ads all say it removes smells.'
Priya: 'Here's what P&G learned with Febreze in 1996: nobody buys a product to admit their house stinks.'
Ethan: 'So what did they do?'
Priya: 'Their cue was invisible. People who live with a smell can't smell it anymore, so nothing triggered daily use. The spray sat in the back of closets.'
Ethan: 'Then how did they ever sell it?'
Priya: 'They repositioned it as the reward at the end of cleaning, the nice smell after you've made the bed or vacuumed. The tagline became Cleans life's smells.'
Ethan: 'So I should stop selling odor elimination entirely?'
Priya: 'Stop leading with it. Make FreshFinish the pleasant finish to a routine people already have, so they start to crave that finish. That craving is what makes the habit loop spin.'
choices: Keep the odor-elimination message but double the advertising budget and give out more free samples.
Reposition FreshFinish as the satisfying final touch of a cleaning routine and pitch the craving for a fresh-smelling finish.
Remove the scent from the product entirely so it is purely functional, and emphasize its scientific efficacy.
Market the spray mainly to people with strong pet odors, since they have the most obvious need.
assets.theoretical_principle: The chapter's insight that invisible cues kill habits, plus the repositioning of the reward to the end of an existing routine to create craving.
assets.psychological_breakdown: The optimal choice mirrors the Febreze relaunch: since bad smells are invisible to the people who live with them, the cue must come from an existing routine such as cleaning a room, and the product becomes the reward, the pleasant smell at the end. That creates the craving that spins the loop and drives repurchase. More advertising of an invisible cue, a scentless functional product, or targeting only pet owners repeats the original failure.

chapters.title: 3. The Golden Rule of Habit Change: Why Transformation Occurs

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Cue, Routine, or Reward: Sorting the Habit Loop
assets.visual_frame_description: A control-room sorting board lights up three lanes labeled Cue, Routine, and Reward. Floating cards show fragments of the chapter's stories: Mandy's fingertip tension, Regan Upshaw's glance at a lineman's foot, John Lynch sprinting to his spot on the field. A pulsing cue-routine-reward loop diagram loops in the corner of the screen as the player drags each card into a lane.
assets.player_mission: Sort every story fragment into the correct part of the three-step habit loop. Each correct placement sharpens your diagnosis of how the loop works; misplacements trigger a brief replay of the loop diagram so you can recalibrate.
key_concepts: A habit is a three-step loop of cue, routine, and reward.
The Golden Rule of habit change holds that a bad habit cannot be extinguished, only changed.
To change a habit you keep the old cue and deliver the old reward while inserting a new routine.
Mandy's nail biting was cued by a tension in her fingertips.
The reward Mandy sought from biting was a brief sense of completeness and physical stimulation.
Mandy replaced biting with a competing response such as putting her hands in her pockets or gripping a pencil.
Defensive end Regan Upshaw focused only on the cues Dungy taught him, such as the opposite lineman's foot and shoulders.
Safety John Lynch read cues like the quarterback's face mask and the spacing of receivers before the ball arrived.
Alcoholics crave escape, relaxation, and companionship more than the intoxication itself.
Dungy attacked only the middle step of the loop, the routine, in his players.
Champions do ordinary things without thinking, too fast for the other team to react.
When players think too much or hesitate, Dungy's system falls apart.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the cue-routine-reward structure of the habit loop: a cue triggers a routine that delivers a reward, and the loop is stored in the basal ganglia. The chapter's Golden Rule states that habits cannot be extinguished, only changed, by keeping the same cue and reward while inserting a new routine.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Classify each story fragment into the correct part of the three-step habit loop described in the chapter.

rows.label: Mandy's tension in her fingertips just before she bites
Mandy putting her hands in her pockets when the tension appears
The brief sense of completeness Mandy feels after working through all her nails
Regan Upshaw checking the outside foot of the opposite lineman
John Lynch running to his assigned spot and waiting for his cue
The escape and relaxation alcoholics crave from drinking
Derrick Brooks reading the movement of the guard before reacting

distractors: The escape and relaxation alcoholics crave is a cue, not a reward.
Mandy's hands-in-pockets action is the reward that ends her loop.
Regan Upshaw's glance at the lineman's foot is a routine, not a cue.
assets.explanation: Mandy's fingertip tension is the cue: it reliably precedes the biting routine and stops mattering once the behavior starts, exactly what awareness training taught her to track. Sorting correctly rests on the chapter's claim that every habit is a three-step loop of cue, routine, and reward, and that change happens only when the middle step, the routine, is reworked.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Applying the Golden Rule: Keeping Cue and Reward
assets.visual_frame_description: A workbench scene shows three trays labeled Golden Rule Applied, Willpower-Only, and Misapplied Change. Cards depicting change attempts from the chapter slide down a chute: Mandy's competing response, the foul-tasting polish, AA's sponsor calls, push-ups for cravings. The player drops each card into the tray that matches how well the attempt preserves the old cue and reward.
assets.player_mission: Judge each change attempt and drop it into the correct tray: does it keep the cue and reward while swapping the routine, does it rely on willpower alone, or does it alter the cue or reward instead of the routine? Correct judgments reveal the Golden Rule in action.
key_concepts: You can never truly extinguish a bad habit; you can only change it.
If you use the same cue and provide the same reward, you can shift the routine and change the habit.
Attempts to give up snacking often fail unless a new routine satisfies the old cue and reward urges.
A smoker usually cannot quit unless she finds an activity to replace cigarettes when her nicotine craving is triggered.
Mandy's foul-tasting nail polish and promises of willpower did not stop her biting.
Mandy's competing response kept the tension cue and the stimulation reward while changing the routine.
AA is, in essence, a giant machine for changing habit loops.
AA gives members sponsor calls and meetings that offer as much escape and catharsis as a Friday night bender.
Studies of former smokers find that choosing new routines that provide similar payoffs makes quitting more likely.
Dungy used the same cues players already had but gave them different routines that became automatic.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the Golden Rule of habit change: to alter a habit you keep the old cue and deliver the old reward while inserting a new routine, because habits cannot be erased. The chapter shows the rule underpinning AA, habit reversal training, and Dungy's coaching, and that willpower-only attempts fail because the old cue and craving remain unaddressed.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: For each change attempt, classify whether it correctly applies the Golden Rule of habit change, relies on willpower without a replacement routine, or misapplies the rule by altering the cue or reward.
assets.column_a_label: Golden Rule applied (same cue, same reward, new routine)
assets.column_c_label: Misapplied change (alters the cue or reward)

rows.label: Mandy puts her hands in her pockets when she feels the fingertip tension, keeping the stimulation reward
Mandy's earlier attempts with foul-tasting nail polish and promises of willpower
A smoker does a quick series of push-ups when the nicotine craving is triggered
A smoker adds afternoon caffeine to satisfy the stimulation the cigarettes provided
AA gives members sponsor calls and meetings that offer escape and catharsis instead of a bar
An alcoholic repeats 'I just need more willpower' while adding no new routine
A dieter swaps chips for candy at 3 p.m. without addressing the boredom that drives the snack

distractors: Keeping the same cue and reward while swapping the routine is a violation of the Golden Rule.
Eliminating the reward entirely is the surest way to change a habit.
Changing the cue while keeping the old routine is the recommended approach.
assets.explanation: Mandy's competing response is the exemplar: the cue (fingertip tension) and reward (quick physical stimulation) stay intact while the routine changes to hands-in-pockets, which is the Golden Rule verbatim: keep the old cue, deliver the old reward, insert a new routine. Her earlier polish-and-willpower attempts lacked any replacement routine, which is exactly why they failed.

assets.topic: The Real Craving: Escape, Stimulation, or the Surface Payoff
assets.visual_frame_description: Three diagnostic stations light up: Escape and Relief, Stimulation and Interruption, and Surface Physical Effect. Patients' craving reports scroll across a triage screen: an alcoholic who drinks to forget work worries, Mandy nibbling during a boring lecture, a smoker reaching for a cigarette during a lull. The player routes each report to the craving category it really reflects.
assets.player_mission: Route each craving report to the correct category. The chapter argues the surface behavior is often not the real reward, so your job is to identify the craving actually driving each habit loop.
key_concepts: Alcoholics crave a drink because it offers escape, relaxation, companionship, and the blunting of anxieties.
Alcoholics might crave a cocktail to forget their worries, but they do not necessarily crave feeling drunk.
The physical effects of alcohol are often one of the least rewarding parts of drinking for addicts.
Mandy bit her nails when she was bored and sought physical stimulation.
Mandy never realized that a craving for physical stimulation was causing her nail biting.
People snack at work not to satisfy hunger but to interrupt boredom.
If you snack for a brief release, a quick walk or three minutes on the Internet provides the same interruption.
Smokers may smoke not for nicotine but for a burst of stimulation, a structure to the day, or a way to socialize.
Ulf Mueller found that relief cravings occur in different parts of the brain than the craving for physical pleasure.
More than three dozen studies of former smokers show that identifying cues and rewards helps quitting.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the distinction between the surface behavior and the craving that actually drives a habit loop. The chapter reports that alcoholics crave escape, relief, and companionship rather than intoxication, and that people snack or smoke to interrupt boredom or provide stimulation, so identifying the true craving is the first step toward a replacement routine.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Sort each craving report into the category that best matches the real reward driving the habit, according to the chapter.
assets.column_c_label: Surface physical effect (often not the real reward)

rows.label: Alcoholics drink to forget their worries and blunt their anxieties
Alcoholics drink for companionship and emotional release
Mandy bites her nails for physical stimulation when she is bored
People snack at work to interrupt boredom rather than satisfy hunger
Smokers use cigarettes for a burst of stimulation and a structure to the day
Assuming that intoxication itself is what alcoholics really crave
The physical effects of alcohol being the least rewarding part of drinking for addicts

distractors: The intoxication itself is the true reward alcoholics chase.
Hunger, not interruption, is why people snack at work.
Nicotine alone explains why smokers reach for cigarettes.
assets.explanation: Mandy's case sorts to stimulation: she never realized a craving for physical stimulation caused her biting, and her reward was that brief physical completeness. The distinction matters because identifying the true craving, escape and relief versus stimulation versus the surface physical effect, is the first step the book prescribes for finding a replacement routine.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Habit Reversal: Awareness, Competing Response, and Preserved Reward
assets.visual_frame_description: A therapy office scene shows the Mississippi State counseling room where Mandy was treated. A progress chart on the wall tracks check marks and hash marks across weeks. Three labeled shelves await classified items: Awareness Training, Competing Response, and Preserved Reward, and the player places each of Mandy's treatment actions onto the right shelf.
assets.player_mission: Sort each technique from Mandy's habit reversal treatment into the correct category. Distinguishing awareness, the competing response, and the preserved reward shows how the Golden Rule operates inside a clinical protocol.
key_concepts: Asking patients to describe what triggers their behavior is called awareness training.
Awareness training is the first step in habit reversal training.
The tension Mandy felt in her nails cued her nail-biting habit.
Most people's habits have occurred for so long they stop noticing what causes them.
Mandy carried an index card and made a check mark each time she felt the cue of fingertip tension.
Mandy came back a week later with twenty-eight checks.
A competing response is an action that makes the old habit impossible, such as putting hands in pockets or gripping a pencil.
Mandy was told to search for something providing quick physical stimulation, like rubbing her arm or rapping her knuckles on a desk.
The cues and rewards stayed the same for Mandy; only the routine changed.
Nathan Azrin, a developer of habit reversal training, said the brain can be reprogrammed if you are deliberate about it.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the three components of habit reversal training: awareness training to identify the cue, a competing response as the new routine, and preservation of the old reward. The chapter shows how Mandy's nail biting was cured once the tension cue and stimulation reward were recognized and a competing routine was inserted, leaving the loop's cue and reward untouched.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Classify each technique used in Mandy's habit reversal treatment into the correct category.

rows.label: The therapist asks Mandy what she feels right before her hand rises to her mouth
Mandy tallies twenty-eight fingertip-tension cues on an index card in a single week
Mandy immediately puts her hands in her pockets when the tension starts
Mandy grips a pencil so she cannot bring her fingers to her mouth
Mandy rubs her arm or raps her knuckles on a desk to produce a quick physical sensation
The therapist places Mandy in front of the television and at homework to watch her bite
The brief completeness Mandy felt after working through all her nails

distractors: Asking a client to describe the trigger is a competing response, not awareness training.
Gripping a pencil is an act of awareness training.
Rubbing one's arm for stimulation removes the old reward rather than preserving it.
assets.explanation: The therapist's question is awareness training, the step that habit reversal developers say is halfway to changing a habit once cues and rewards are recognized. Mandy's sequence shows awareness first, then the competing response, with the reward intentionally preserved so the loop keeps functioning.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Routine, Belief, or Community: What Makes Change Stick
assets.visual_frame_description: A church basement AA meeting in Brooklyn fills the screen, with folding chairs and a podium where John tells his story. Three totems stand beside the room: a New Routine card, a Belief lantern, and a Community circle of people. The player classifies evidence from the chapter into whichever totem best explains each part of lasting change.
assets.player_mission: Sort each factor in permanent habit change into the correct category: a new routine, the belief that change is possible, or the community where that belief forms. Correct classification explains why replacement habits sometimes fail under stress.
key_concepts: Replacement habits only become durable new behaviors when they are accompanied by belief.
Researchers concluded it was not God that mattered but belief itself that made the difference.
Once people learned how to believe in something, that skill started spilling over to other parts of their lives.
Belief is the ingredient that made a reworked habit loop into a permanent behavior.
Belief is easier when it occurs within a community.
For most people who overhaul their lives there are no seminal moments, only communities that make change believable.
Psychologist Todd Heatherton said change occurs among other people and seems real when we can see it in other people's eyes.
Lee Ann Kaskutas said a community creates belief and helps people suspend disbelief about their own change.
The Magdeburg patients relapsed after stressful events until they learned alternate routines for coping with stress.
A habit cannot be eradicated; it must instead be replaced.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the three ingredients of lasting change: a replacement routine, belief that change is possible, and the community where that belief forms. assets.scenario_setup: Sam, 38, an IT service manager, wants to quit smoking. Every cigarette follows a frustrating meeting and gives him a burst of stimulation and a marker that the stressful stretch of his day is over. You: And what exactly happens in that moment on Thursday?
Sam: I'll be leaving a meeting where my boss chewed me out and I just want a second to breathe. The cigarette is that second.
You: So the cigarette is less about nicotine and more about a burst of stimulation and a reset after stress.
Sam: Yeah, I think so. If I don't have it, the day never feels like it lets up.
You: What if the reset came from something that isn't a cigarette, but happens at the exact same moment?
Sam: Like what? I can't step out of a building mid-crisis.
You: You don't have to. A few quick push-ups against the wall, or two minutes of stretching by the window, right when the meeting ends.

Advise Sam to identify the craving (stimulation and a reset after stress), keep the same cue and reward, and insert a new routine such as push-ups or stretching at the moment the meeting ends.

assets.scenario_setup: Your friend Lena, 44, a hospital administrator, quit smoking nine months ago using a plan she built with a support group of former smokers. Last month her father was diagnosed with advanced cancer, and within a week she was smoking again. She is meeting you at a café, half-apologetic and half-defeated, wondering whether going back to the group will do any good since she already knows all the routines.

You: You're not a fraud. The routines worked for nine months, and that's the point. They work until the stress gets too high.
Lena: Then what's the use? My dad is sick. The stress isn't going anywhere.
You: The research on this is pretty clear. The routines are only half of it. The other half is believing you can get through the bad day without the cigarette.
Lena: I used to believe that. In the group I believed it. Alone at midnight, not so much.
You: Exactly. That's why the group exists, not just for the tricks but for watching other people make it through, so you can believe you can too.

You: I think you should walk back in before the next hard moment, and tell them exactly what happened. That's what the group is there for.

Tell Lena that going back to the group is exactly right, because belief is the ingredient that makes a changed habit durable under stress, and belief grows inside a community that has watched others change.
Advise Lena to quit the group and simply add a stronger routine, like running, because a better routine will fix the relapse.

key_concepts: Keystone habits are the habits that, when they start to shift, dislodge and remake other patterns.

The book argues the email network illustrates the structure pathway because it was a platform built for safety that carried other habits along with it.

That matches the New Structures pathway: keystone habits create structures that help other habits flourish, exactly as O'Neill intended.
