assets.topic: Planning around inflection points
assets.visual_frame_description: A Scottish orthopedic hospital where a psychologist hands five dozen elderly patients a rehab booklet with thirteen blank weekly pages headed 'My goals for this week are...'. Two patients sit in identical hospital gowns: one writes detailed plans for walking to the bus stop, while the other leaves the pages blank and stares out the window. A stopwatch later times them walking and rising from chairs, with the planners finishing far ahead.
assets.player_mission: Defeat the Relapse-Resolve boss by identifying what the planners achieved versus the non-planners, then design a workbook that focuses patients on the moments where pain and the temptation to quit peak. Answer both stages to clear the battle.
key_concepts: The Scottish study recruited five dozen patients from two of Scotland's busiest orthopedic hospitals who had recently undergone hip or knee replacement surgery.
The patients averaged sixty-eight years old, most earned less than $10,000 a year, and many had waited years for their operations.
Each patient received a booklet with thirteen blank weekly pages asking them to write down exactly what they were going to do, such as where and when they would walk.
Patients who wrote out goals started walking almost twice as fast as patients who did not write anything.
The planners got in and out of chairs unassisted almost three times as fast and were quicker at dressing, doing laundry, and making meals.
Most of the winning plans focused on how patients would handle a specific moment of anticipated pain, their inflection points.
One patient exercised every time he went to the bathroom, scheduling very specific routines around a painful moment.
The bus-stop patient detailed every obstacle he might confront and came up with a solution ahead of time.
The plans gave patients a simple cue and an obvious reward, the same structure Claude Hopkins used to sell Pepsodent.
The non-planners were not at a knowledge disadvantage; they simply never deliberately designed willpower habits, so their resolve abandoned them at the first painful steps.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests implementation planning at inflection points, the claim that resolve fails at moments of pain unless a concrete routine has been chosen in advance. Scottish hip and knee replacement patients who wrote specific weekly plans walked almost twice as fast and rose from chairs almost three times as fast as patients who wrote nothing, because their plans targeted the exact moments when the temptation to quit peaked.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the 1992 Scottish orthopedic study's finding that writing concrete plans for anticipated inflection points dramatically speeds recovery, because the plans convert resolve into automatic routines.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are the psychologist who handed five dozen elderly patients, mostly sixty-eight-year-olds earning under $10,000 a year, a rehab booklet with thirteen blank weekly pages: 'My goals for this week are...'. Some patients fill every page with specific plans; others leave the pages blank. All received the same surgical care and warnings about the importance of exercise.
assets.stage_1_question: Three months later you compare the two groups. What did the planners achieve that the non-planners did not?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The patients who wrote out plans started walking almost twice as fast, got in and out of chairs unassisted almost three times as fast, and dressed, did laundry, and cooked meals more quickly. Both groups knew exercise was essential, so the difference came from the deliberate planning, not from knowledge or motivation.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Reviewing the booklets, you notice the winning plans share a structure. You must now design the next cohort's workbook. What should your instructions emphasize so the plans actually hold up at the moment of pain?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Instruct patients to build plans around inflection points: the exact moments when they know pain and the temptation to quit will be strongest, with a specific response for each. The bus-stop man detailed his route, coat, rain plan, and pain pills; the bathroom man planned to take the first step automatically before he could sit back down. These are the cue-and-reward structures that become willpower habits.

assets.topic: Autonomy in the workplace
assets.visual_frame_description: An Ohio assembly plant where workers in self-designed uniforms adjust their own shifts while a productivity chart climbs 20 percent over two months. Beside it, a Starbucks store where partners debate where to place a blender, move espresso machines, and choose how customers are greeted, with turnover and satisfaction graphs trending in opposite directions. Muraren's lab replay shows kindly versus brusquely treated students on the vigilance test.
assets.player_mission: Defeat the Willpower-Fatigue boss by identifying what separated the students who kept their focus, then choose the workplace change that best reproduces the Ohio plant's 20 percent productivity jump. Answer both stages to clear the battle.
key_concepts: Muraven's kindly treated students retained their willpower on the 6-followed-by-4 vigilance test because they felt a sense of control over their experience.
When people think they are doing something for personal reasons, because it is a choice or because it helps someone else, it is much less taxing than following orders.
If people feel they have no autonomy and are just following orders, their willpower muscles get tired much faster.
In the cookie experiment, students treated like cogs rather than people needed a lot more willpower to ignore the treats.

A 2010 study at a manufacturing plant in Ohio empowered assembly-line workers to make small decisions about their schedules and work environment, such as designing their own uniforms and controlling their shifts.
With nothing else changed, productivity at the Ohio plant increased by 20 percent within two months, and workers took shorter breaks and made fewer mistakes.
Giving employees a sense of agency, a feeling they are in control with genuine decision-making authority, can radically increase the energy and focus they bring to their jobs.
Starbucks has asked workers to redesign how espresso machines and cash registers are laid out and to decide how customers are greeted and where merchandise is displayed.
It is not unusual for a Starbucks store manager to spend hours discussing with employees where a blender should be located.
Since these changes, turnover has gone down, customer satisfaction is up, and Starbucks has boosted revenues by more than $1.2 billion per year.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the autonomy effect in organizations, the claim that a genuine sense of control reduces the cost of self-discipline and increases focus. Muraren's kindly treated students outlasted ordered students on a vigilance test, and an Ohio plant where workers controlled uniforms and shifts raised productivity 20 percent in two months with no other changes.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the book's claim that giving people a genuine sense of control and decision-making authority reduces the cost of self-discipline and increases the energy and focus they bring to work.
assets.stage_1_observation: You are Muraven at the University of Albany. Undergraduates must ignore a plate of warm cookies. You greet half of them warmly, explain the experiment's purpose, thank them, and invite their suggestions; you order the other half around with no explanation. Then everyone takes a twelve-minute computer vigilance test, hitting the space bar whenever a 6 is followed by a 4.
assets.stage_1_question: Both groups resisted the cookies, yet their subsequent performance diverged sharply. What best explains the gap?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The students who were treated kindly and given a sense of control maintained focus for the full twelve minutes, while the brusquely ordered students forgot to hit the space bar and said they were too tired. Muraven found the key difference was the sense of control students had over their experience: doing something for personal reasons is much less taxing than following orders, and being treated like cogs drains the willpower muscle faster.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You manage an assembly line. A 2010 Ohio study showed productivity jumped 20 percent within two months when workers were empowered to make small decisions about their schedules and work environment, with nothing else changed. Starbucks now lets partners redesign espresso-machine layouts and decide how customers are greeted. Which change should you pilot first to boost self-discipline on the floor?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Grant workers genuine, meaningful decisions over their own work, such as designing their own uniforms, setting their own shifts, or laying out their own stations, while keeping processes and pay the same. The chapter shows this alone raised productivity 20 percent, shortened breaks, and cut mistakes, because a sense of agency reduces the willpower cost of showing up disciplined.

assets.topic: The LATTE method in action
assets.visual_frame_description: At 8:10 a.m. in a Starbucks on Fort Washington in Fresno, a new barista named Marcus faces a furious customer, Dana, who slams a venti caramel macchiato on the counter because it tastes burnt and her name is misspelled. Travis, the store manager, watches from the end of the bar, one hand resting on a training workbook opened to the page 'When a customer is unhappy, my plan is to...'. A line of customers waits behind Dana, and the register light blinks.
assets.player_mission: Step into Marcus's shoes and run the LATTE loop: Listen, Acknowledge, Take action, Thank, and Explain. Choose the response that de-escalates Dana and turns the exchange into evidence of a job well done instead of a blowup.
key_concepts: Starbucks workbook pages read 'When a customer is unhappy, my plan is to...' and employees fill them out in advance.
The LATTE method is to Listen to the customer, Acknowledge their complaint, Take action by solving the problem, Thank them, and Explain why the problem occurred.
Willpower becomes a habit by choosing a behavior ahead of time and following that routine when an inflection point arrives.
Starbucks trains employees to deliver a bit of joy alongside lattes and scones because people expect an expensive latte delivered with a bit of sparkle.
Howard Behar said: 'We're not in the coffee business serving people; we're in the people business serving coffee.'
Employees are rewarded by a grateful customer or praise from a manager as evidence of a job well done.
Before Starbucks, Travis lost control at drive-throughs, once throwing chicken nuggets at a woman's car and shouting at her to get out of his drive-through.
Travis now tells employees 'Your apron is a shield' and that nothing anyone says will ever hurt them.
Without trained baristas, the emotions of some employees inevitably spill into how they treat customers.
Managers drill employees by role-playing until the responses become automatic.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue simulates the LATTE willpower habit loop, the claim that choosing a behavior ahead of time lets an employee run a calm routine at the angry-customer inflection point instead of snapping. Marcus's pre-written plan converts a four-dollar complaint into a de-escalated exchange with a grateful customer as the reward, the exact training that rebuilt Travis Leach's self-control.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: It is 8:10 a.m. at a Starbucks on Fort Washington in Fresno, during the morning rush. Marcus, a new barista who was fired from a car wash for insubordination before joining Starbucks, is at the register. Dana slams a venti caramel macchiato on the counter, furious that it tastes burnt and that her name is misspelled. Travis, the store manager, watches from the end of the bar. Marcus has just filled in the workbook page 'When a customer is unhappy, my plan is to...' and studied the LATTE method. His goal is to de-escalate the exchange without snapping the way he used to at McDonald's, and to give Travis evidence of a job well done. The stakes: a four-dollar latte that a customer expects to come with a bit of sparkle, and a line of customers waiting behind Dana.
dialogue: Travis: 'Marcus, she's already gone sideways. This is the page in your workbook: When a customer is unhappy, my plan is to... What does the first step say?'
Marcus: 'Listen to the customer.'
Dana: 'I said oat milk, not two percent. And I watched you scribble the wrong name before you even rang me up!'
Travis: 'Good, you're listening. Now acknowledge the complaint. Don't argue with her. Tell her you hear it.'
Dana: 'Are you even paying attention? I'm about to walk out and never come back.'
Travis: 'This is the inflection point, Marcus. Run the loop.'
choices: I hear you, and you're right to be annoyed. You waited and got the wrong drink. Let me make a fresh one with oat milk right now, on the house. Thanks for telling me, and I'm sorry the sticker on the screen showed the wrong name.
Ma'am, it's 8 a.m. and there's a line. If you'd spoken up sooner, I could have fixed it.
It's not my fault. Your name isn't even spelled like that on the cup, but it's just coffee, okay?
Say nothing, push the drink back across the counter, and turn to the register to take the next customer's order.
assets.theoretical_principle: The LATTE method (Listen, Acknowledge, Take action, Thank, Explain) and the willpower habit loop: choosing a behavior ahead of time and following it when an inflection point arrives.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 works because it executes every step of the pre-written LATTE plan: it listens and acknowledges the complaint, takes immediate action with a free remake in the right milk, thanks Dana, and explains why the sticker was wrong, so the angry-customer cue triggers a calm routine rather than an emotional reaction, and Dana walks away a grateful customer, the named reward. Choice 1 fails because dismissing her complaint escalates the inflection point and discards the routine. Choice 2 fails because defending yourself is the old pre-Starbucks response that got Travis fired from McDonald's and Hollywood Video. Choice 3 fails because avoidance abandons the loop entirely, leaving Dana angrier and the line more tense.

assets.topic: The What What Why system of criticism
assets.visual_frame_description: At closing time in a Starbucks in Sacramento, Janelle, a shift partner of nine months, sits at a back table clutching a crumpled apron, her eyes red from crying after a customer screamed at her and she screamed back. Travis, the store manager, pulls up a chair across from her with a training manual open to the What What Why section. The district manager's number glows on a phone screen on the table between them.
assets.player_mission: Step into Travis's role and deliver feedback through the What What Why system: state what happened, what the correct behavior is, and why it matters, then commit to drilling the routine. Choose the response that builds Janelle's self-discipline instead of shredding it.
key_concepts: Starbucks teaches the What What Why system of giving criticism.
The company developed training materials that spelled out routines for employees to use when they hit rough patches.
Employees with willpower lapses had no difficulty doing their jobs most of the time, but snapped under unexpected stress or uncertainty.
Starbucks identified specific rewards, such as a grateful customer or praise from a manager, that employees could look to as evidence of a job well done.
Travis himself used to start crying in the middle of shifts and yell at his reflection in the mirror, ordering himself to be better.
Travis's hands would start shaking and he could not catch his breath when a line got long and a manager shouted.
The training program began on Travis's first day and continues throughout an employee's career, structured enough to earn college credits.
Managers role-play with employees until the responses become automatic.
The book states this is how willpower becomes a habit: choosing a behavior ahead of time and following the routine when the inflection point arrives.
Howard Behar said the entire business model is based on fantastic customer service and that without it, the company is toast.
assets.theory_summary: This dialogue simulates the What What Why system of giving criticism, the claim that feedback must name what happened, what the correct behavior is, and why it matters so an employee can build a routine for the inflection point instead of relying on raw resolve. When paired with role-play, the criticism converts a self-control lapse into a drilled, automatic response, the same process that rebuilt Travis Leach's composure.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: At closing time in a Starbucks in Sacramento, Janelle, a shift partner of nine months, tells Travis what happened: a customer screamed at her over a spilled order and she screamed right back, then started crying in the back. Travis remembers how he used to lose control the same way at McDonald's and Hollywood Video, yelling at his reflection in the mirror to be better and failing. He has to deliver criticism that builds Janelle's self-discipline instead of shredding it, using the What What Why system. The stakes: if she cannot handle one angry customer she will fail in a job built on fantastic customer service, but if Travis only punishes her she will learn nothing about the routine that could have saved her.
dialogue: Janelle: 'Travis, I'm sorry. He was screaming about his drink and I screamed back, and then I went in the back and cried. I feel like I'm back at my last job all over again.'
Janelle: 'I keep telling myself to be better, to suck it up, but when the line gets long and someone shouts at me my hands start shaking.'
Travis: 'You did control yourself for most of the shift, Janelle. You just didn't have a plan for that exact moment. I know that feeling.'
Janelle: 'Then what am I supposed to do when it happens again? Because it will happen again.'
Travis: 'Now we build the plan. What happened, what should happen instead, and why it matters.'
Janelle: 'And if I freeze up anyway?'
Travis: 'Then you run the loop anyway. That is what the drill is for.'
choices: What happened is that when your tray was spilled, you matched his volume. What should have happened is the LATTE loop: listen, acknowledge, take action, thank, and explain, and then hand him his fresh drink no matter how loud he gets. Why it matters is this company runs on fantastic customer service, and a barista who can hold her composure through a screaming customer is the whole business. Now let's role-play it until it's automatic.
What happened is you're not cut out for the register. What should have happened is you shouldn't have spilled his tray in the first place. Why it matters is we can't have partners crying in the back.
It's fine, it happens to everyone. Let's just get through the rest of the shift and I won't mention it to the district manager.
You need to be tougher, Janelle. When a customer yells, you yell right back. Customers respect someone who stands up for themselves.
assets.theoretical_principle: The What What Why system of giving criticism combined with the willpower habit loop: criticism should specify what happened, what the correct behavior is, and why it matters, so the employee can build a pre-chosen routine for the inflection point instead of relying on raw resolve.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 0 is the complete What What Why: it states what happened, prescribes the LATTE routine as what should have happened, explains why fantastic customer service matters, and closes by drilling the plan until it is automatic, which is exactly how the chapter says willpower becomes a habit. Choice 1 fails because it attacks Janelle's identity instead of her behavior and gives her no replacement routine. Choice 2 fails because minimizing the incident hands her no plan for the next inflection point, guaranteeing a repeat. Choice 3 fails because it reinforces the very impulse-control failure that got Travis fired from earlier jobs, treating raw toughness as the answer when the book shows the answer is a drilled routine.

chapters.title: 6. The Power of a Crisis: How Leaders Create Habits Through Accident : and Design

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Keystone habits, accidental toxic habits, and balanced truce routines
assets.visual_frame_description: Three columns slide onto the screen above an illustrated corporate campus. The left column is stamped in green with a plant manager at a safety briefing; the middle column is tinted red with a hospital hallway whiteboard listing doctors' names in blue, red, and black; the right column is tinted blue with a London Underground ticket booth and a distant escalator. Evidence cards drift down from the top and the player drags each one into the column it belongs to.
assets.player_mission: Sort each institutional pattern into the column it best represents: deliberately designed keystone habits, habits that grew by accident from fear and rivalry, or balanced-truce routines. Assign every evidence card before the timer expires to reveal how the same habit machinery can either cascade into success or collapse into disaster.
key_concepts: At Alcoa, CEO Paul O'Neill made worker safety the firm's top measure, and that single keystone habit cascaded into productivity and profit gains.
Rhode Island Hospital's habits were not deliberately planned; they grew by accident and spread through whispered warnings until toxic patterns emerged.
Nurses at Rhode Island Hospital used color-coded whiteboards - blue for 'nice', red for 'jerk', and black for doctors you should never contradict.
Inside the London Underground, ticketing clerks were ordered to stay in their booths and sell tickets, which eliminated long lines but left them unable to watch for fire.
The London fire brigade insisted on using its own street-level hydrants because a decade earlier firemen had wasted precious minutes on unfamiliar pipes.
Institutions develop informal rules - habits unique to the organization - that help avert the most obvious conflicts.
Habits that are deliberately designed create larger and larger successes, while the wrong ones can create disasters.
Rhode Island Hospital's corrosive culture produced a one-sided truce in which nurses absorbed abuse while doctors rarely learned their names.
The eighty-six-year-old patient died after surgeons opened the wrong side of his head because no one stopped to verify the consent form.
Just as choosing the right keystone habits can create amazing change, the wrong ones can create disasters.

key_concepts: In November 1987, a commuter told Philip Brickell about a burning tissue at the bottom of a Piccadilly escalator at King's Cross.

No one person, department, or baron had ultimate responsibility for passengers' safety.

key_concepts: Organizational habits offer a basic promise: follow the established patterns and the truce, and rivalries won't destroy the company.

An ambitious executive could kill a sale with one quiet phone call to sabotage a colleague's division.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The central concept: organizational routines create truces that require individuals to give up short-term advantage for collective survival - the salesperson who follows the discount truce keeps the firm and her own bonus alive.
assets.stage_1_observation: Maya, a salesperson at a mid-sized consumer goods firm, knows that a single hefty discount could land her the biggest client of the year and a fat bonus. But she also knows the firm's January tradition: all salespeople agree to limit how many discounts they offer, precisely so the company doesn't go bankrupt and everyone gets a raise at year-end.
assets.stage_1_question: Why does the group's January agreement exist, and what would happen if every salesperson pursued the same short-term win Maya is tempted by?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The agreement is an organizational truce that trades individual discounting for collective survival; if everyone gave away hefty discounts the firm would go bankrupt and there would be no bonuses at all, so the routine exists to keep rivalry within bounds.
assets.stage_2_intervention: An executive is watching. Maya quietly calculates that one under-the-table discount would seal the deal without anyone knowing. She must decide whether to honor the truce.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Maya should honor the truce and stick to the discount limits - the book shows the promise at the heart of organizational habits: follow the established patterns and the truce, and rivalries won't destroy the company, profits roll in, and everyone eventually gets taken care of.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: The time-out confrontation
assets.visual_frame_description: The scene is a surgery suite during a time-out. The OR nurse stands at the center of a gathered team, while the surgeon pivots toward the door, one hand on the handle and his back to the checklist. The player, as the nurse, watches his body language and a dialogue bar offers response options in real time.
assets.player_mission: Lead the time-out confrontation with the surgeon in real time. Read his escalating pushback and choose the response that keeps the safety routine intact without needlessly inflaming the exchange, then explain how each choice reshapes the hospital's truce.
key_concepts: Time-outs are standard procedure at most hospitals, a way for doctors and staff to make sure mistakes are avoided.
A surgeon at Rhode Island Hospital had accidentally removed the tonsils of a girl who was supposed to have eye surgery.
When the OR nurse asked the team to gather for a time-out, the surgeon headed for the doors.
'Why don't you lead this?' the surgeon told the nurse. 'I'm going to step outside for a call.'
The nurse replied, 'You're supposed to be here for this, Doctor.'
The surgeon said, 'If I want your damn opinion, I'll ask for it. Don't ever question my authority again.'
The nurse led the time-out and retrieved the doctor, and the procedure occurred without complication.
She never contradicted a physician again, and never said anything when other safety policies were ignored.
Rhode Island Hospital's routines appeared by accident and spread through whispered warnings until toxic patterns emerged.
The hospital's institutional habits were so dysfunctional that a grievous mistake seemed inevitable.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the corrosive effect of one-sided truces on institutional safety habits. The book shows that when the nurse conceded the time-out to the surgeon, she never contradicted a physician again, deepening the toxic pattern.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: You are a surgical nurse at Rhode Island Hospital during an abdominal operation. A time-out is standard procedure, and nursing staff insist on it because a surgeon once removed the tonsils of a girl who was supposed to have eye surgery. As the team gathers around the patient, the surgeon heads for the door: 'Why don't you lead this? I'm going to step outside for a call. Knock when you're ready.' The stakes are high - if you push back, you may face the hospital's corrosive culture; if you stay silent, the safety routine is quietly abandoned.
dialogue: Nurse (you): 'You're supposed to be here for this, Doctor. Time-outs exist to catch mistakes before they happen.'
Surgeon: 'You can handle it. I'll only be a minute.'
Nurse (you): 'Doctor, I don't feel this is appropriate. The team needs to review the plan together.'
Surgeon: 'If I want your damn opinion, I'll ask for it. Don't ever question my authority again. If you can't do your job, get the hell out of my OR.'
Anesthesia tech (aside): 'We're ready whenever the team is. The checklist is still open.'
Surgeon: 'You heard the tech. Either we do this now or I find another room.'
Nurse (you): (choose your response)
choices: Hold your ground: 'I'm not questioning your authority, but I won't run this time-out without you. The standard is that the whole team participates - please stay.'
Apologize and lead the time-out alone so the surgery can proceed.
Say nothing, note the breach in your chart, and continue preparing the instruments.
Leave the room and call the nursing supervisor to complain.
assets.theoretical_principle: One-sided truces and the corrosive culture of institutions whose habits are not deliberately designed.
assets.psychological_breakdown: The optimal choice holds the line on the safety routine while keeping the exchange professional - it refuses to let the surgeon's dominance convert a two-sided safety ritual into a one-sided truce. Apologizing and leading alone (option 1) is what actually happened in the book, and it taught the nurse never to contradict a physician again, deepening the toxic pattern. Silence (option 2) quietly normalizes the abandonment of the time-out, and escalating to a supervisor (option 3) sidesteps the moment of intervention the routine exists for, so neither repairs the habit.

assets.topic: Questioning a surgeon's wrong-side order
assets.visual_frame_description: The scene freezes on the moment the nurse picks up the consent form and chart in a rushing OR. The elderly man's head is already cradled on its side, antiseptic being applied, while the surgeon's marker hovers over the paperwork. A red glow outlines the hallway whiteboard and a dialogue interface offers the player four live responses.
assets.player_mission: Navigate the real-time exchange with the surgeon who insists the patient is crashing and wants to proceed on a guess. Choose the response that protects the verification routine, then review why conceding, going silent, or hunting for the family fails the patient.
key_concepts: A nurse picked up the elderly man's consent form and noticed it didn't say where the hematoma was.
Every hospital relies on paperwork; no one is supposed to go into surgery without a signed and detailed consent.
The hospital's computers locked after fifteen minutes of idling, so pulling up the films would take at least a minute.
The surgeon said, 'I saw the scans before. It was the right side of the head.'
The nurse asked, 'Maybe we should pull up the films again.'
The surgeon replied, 'We don't have time... We've got to relieve the pressure.'
The nurse knew the surgeon's name was often written in black on the whiteboard.
The unwritten rules in the scenario were clear: the surgeon always wins.
The surgeon scribbled 'right' on the consent form, initialed it, and ordered the operation to begin.
The nurse put down the chart and stood aside - and the wrong side of the man's head was opened.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests whether verification routines survive when authority is unbalanced. The book's account of the wrong-side operation shows the nurse's deference allowed a fatal error, and that real justice requires routines no single authority can override.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: You are the surgical nurse assisting with the operation on the eighty-six-year-old man with a subdural hematoma. The consent form in your hand does not say which side of the head the surgery is for, and the hospital's computers lock after fifteen minutes of inactivity, so verifying would take at least a minute. The surgeon, whose name is written in black on the hallway whiteboard, insists the patient is crashing and orders you to proceed immediately. Your intervention may be the only thing standing between the man and a fatal wrong-side operation.
dialogue: Nurse (you): 'Doctor, the consent form doesn't say where the hematoma is. We should pull up the films and confirm the side.'
Surgeon: 'I saw the scans before. It was the right side of the head. If we don't do this quickly, he's gonna die.'
Nurse (you): 'It would take about a minute to log in and load the images. I don't want to guess on something like this.'
Surgeon: 'We don't have time. They told me he's crashing. We've got to relieve the pressure.'
Nurse (you): 'Then give me the minute it takes to be sure. If we're wrong, no amount of speed helps him.'
Surgeon: 'I saw the films with my own eyes. Are you refusing an order?'
Nurse (you): (choose your response)
choices: Stand firm: 'I'm not going to hold a scalpel to a skull until we've confirmed the side. Give me the minute to log in - it's faster than the alternative if we're wrong.'
Concede: 'Fine. The scans were clear - right side it is. Proceeding.'
Step aside silently and let the surgeon proceed while you mentally note the discrepancy.
Page the ER to locate the patient's wife and ask her to confirm the side.
assets.theoretical_principle: When truces are unbalanced, routines fail exactly when they are needed most; institutional justice requires verification habits that no single authority can override.
assets.psychological_breakdown: The optimal choice treats the ambiguity as a hard stop and protects the verification routine even against the surgeon's urgency - this is what the one-sided truce at Rhode Island Hospital destroyed, leading to the wrong-side operation and the patient's death. Conceding (option 1) reproduces the fatal error the chapter narrates. Silent compliance (option 2) is the failure mode of the whole culture. Hunting for the family (option 3) spends critical minutes that the films would resolve more directly and still leaves the side unverified.

assets.topic: Sticky songs and the familiarity principle
assets.visual_frame_description: A radio-station analytics suite fills the screen with six scenario cards floating above three drop zones labeled 'Sticky because familiar,' 'Non-sticky novelty,' and 'Algorithm-predicted hit.' A live Arbitron-style tune-out graph pulses behind a Celine Dion card, while a waveform for 'Hey Ya!' flickers with a red 26.6 percent reading.
assets.player_mission: Drag each listening-scenario card into the column that best explains whether listeners stayed tuned or changed the station. Classify all six correctly to complete the playlist audit.
key_concepts: Songs that sound familiar to a listener's existing radio habits are 'sticky' even when listeners say they dislike them.
Male listeners who told pollsters they hated Celine Dion stayed tuned whenever her songs played.
Playing Celine Dion at the end of the hour could boost a Los Angeles station's measured audience by as much as 3 percent.
Rich Meyer, who founded Mediabase, noticed that sticky songs all sounded exactly like what he expected to hear from their genre.
Sticky songs sounded familiar but a little more polished, closer to the golden mean of the perfect song.
Blu Cantrell's 'Breathe' was sticky in summer 2003 even though DJs played it reluctantly and listeners later said they didn't like it.
Early September plays of 'Hey Ya!' drove a 26.6 percent tune-out because the song sounded like nothing else on the radio.
Hit Song Science compared a song's tempo, pitch, melody, and chord progression against thousands of stored hits to forecast its success.
Listening to music activates the auditory cortex, the thalamus, and the superior parietal cortex, which are tied to pattern recognition.
Our brains crave familiar sounds because familiarity is how we manage to hear without becoming overwhelmed by noise.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the familiarity principle in listening habits: audiences reject novelty and stay with songs that sound like what they already expect, because the brain is wired to seek out familiar patterns. Duhigg reports that 'Hey Ya!' lost nearly a third of its listeners within thirty seconds until DJs made it familiar, after which its tune-out factor fell to 5.7 percent.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Sort each listening scenario into the column that best explains why listeners stayed tuned or clicked away.
assets.column_a_label: Sticky because familiar (sounds like everything else on the radio)
assets.column_b_label: Non-sticky novelty (sounds like nothing else on the radio)
assets.column_c_label: Algorithm-predicted hit (high Hit Song Science score)

rows.label: Men who say they hate Celine Dion stay tuned whenever she plays at the end of the hour
Blu Cantrell's bland 'Breathe' keeps listeners from changing the dial in summer 2003
'Hey Ya!' on WIOQ in early September 2003, before the sandwiching starts
Norah Jones's 'Come Away With Me,' which the industry had dismissed
'Hey Ya!' in December 2003, after months of being played between sticky hits
Santana's 'Why Don't You and I,' doubted by DJs yet popular

distractors: Stickiness depends on star power alone; only famous artists keep listeners tuned in.
Listeners actively dislike sticky songs, so radio stations avoid them to grow audiences.
A high Hit Song Science score is a reliable guarantee that listeners will stay tuned from the very first play.
assets.explanation: The Celine Dion row sorts to column a because stickiness is driven by familiarity, not declared taste: male listeners told pollsters they hated Dion, yet stayed tuned whenever she played, and Los Angeles stations that aired her at the end of the hour could boost measured audience by up to 3 percent. Rich Meyer found sticky songs sound exactly like what listeners expect from their genre, so the brain, which craves familiar auditory patterns, keeps listening. 'Hey Ya!' was non-sticky early on (a 26.6 percent tune-out) precisely because it sounded like nothing else, and the high Hit Song Science score in column c was not enough to override that.

assets.topic: Major life events open shopping habits to change
assets.visual_frame_description: A suburban kitchen table is spread with three sorting columns: 'Major life event,' 'Habit persistence,' and 'In-the-moment shelf decision.' Scenario cards show named shoppers, including a woman with a shopping list, a newly married man, and a divorcée, while a tape-recorder icon hints at the grocery-store study that produced the data.
assets.player_mission: Classify each shopper scenario into the column that best explains the behavior. Read each card closely: some shoppers are in transition, some are locked into routines, and some are swayed at the shelf.
key_concepts: Alan Andreasen's 1984 UCLA study used telephone surveys with about three hundred Los Angeles consumers about their recent shopping trips.
In the six months before the study, 10.5 percent of surveyed consumers had switched toothpaste brands.
More than 15 percent of those surveyed had started buying a new kind of laundry detergent.
People's buying habits are more likely to change when they go through a major life event.
Getting married makes people more likely to start buying a new type of coffee.
Moving into a new house makes people more apt to purchase a different kind of cereal.
Getting divorced raises the chance that a person will start buying different brands of beer.
Andreasen found that life changes make consumers more 'vulnerable to intervention by marketers.'
Having a baby is the greatest upheaval and makes new parents' habits more flexible than at almost any other time in adult life.
A 2010 survey estimated the average parent spends $6,800 on baby items before a child's first birthday.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests Andreasen's life-event insight: shopping habits are most malleable during major transitions such as marriage, moving, divorce, or having a baby, which makes consumers 'vulnerable to intervention by marketers.' The book cites his 1984 UCLA findings and applies them to Target's decision to target expectant mothers.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Sort each shopping scenario into the column that best explains the shopper's behavior.
assets.column_a_label: Major life event opens habits to change (vulnerable to marketers)
assets.column_b_label: Habit persistence (automatic repeat despite current goals)
assets.column_c_label: In-the-moment decision at the shelf (stronger than written list)

rows.label: A newly married man starts buying a different brand of coffee
The Folgers woman buys the same coffee month after month even though she admits she isn't crazy about it
A shopper carrying a list grabs the Lay's potato chips because they're on sale
A recently divorced woman switches brands of beer
A family that just moved into a new house starts buying a different kind of cereal
A shopper buys roughly the same amount of food every trip even after pledging to cut back

distractors: Shopping behavior never changes once a person reaches adulthood.
People switch brands only when they discover a product is objectively better.
A shopping list guarantees a shopper will stick to planned purchases.
assets.explanation: The focal scenario sorts to column a because Alan Andreasen's 1984 UCLA research found that buying habits are most likely to change when people go through major life events such as marriage, moving, or divorce, which make consumers 'vulnerable to intervention by marketers.' The Folgers woman and the shopper who buys the same amount each trip belong in column b: habits reigned supreme in most consumers, who automatically repeat past behavior with little regard to current goals. The Lay's shopper belongs in column c because more than 50 percent of purchasing decisions were made at the moment a customer saw a product on the shelf, overriding written intentions.

assets.topic: Sources of consumer data behind the Guest ID
assets.visual_frame_description: A data-warehouse command center shows a glowing Guest ID card at the center with streams of records feeding into it. Cards describe a credit-card swipe, a mailed coupon redemption, a Rapleaf demographic report, and InfiniGraph listening to an online forum, each waiting to be sorted into the three source columns.
assets.player_mission: Sort each data source into the column describing how Target or its partners obtained it. Distinguish what the customer gave Target directly from what was bought or observed.
key_concepts: Target assigned every shopper an identification code known internally as the Guest ID number.
Using a Target-issued credit card, handing over a frequent-buyer tag, or redeeming a mailed coupon was recorded and linked to the Guest ID.
Target's data warehouse also captured surveys, refunds, help-line calls, opened emails, and visits to Target.com.
Target collected or purchased demographic information including age, marital status, income estimate, and whether a shopper had moved recently.
Data peddlers such as InfiniGraph 'listen' to shoppers' online conversations on message boards and Internet forums.
A firm named Rapleaf sells information on shoppers' political leanings, reading habits, and charitable giving.
Some companies analyze photos consumers post online, cataloging if they are obese or skinny, tall or short, hairy or bald.
Tom Davenport said that used to be companies only knew what their customers wanted them to know, and 'that world is far behind us.'
Andrew Pole's mandate was to become a mathematical mind reader, deciphering shoppers' habits to convince them to spend more.
Pole reported Target could link about half of all in-store sales, almost all online sales, and about a quarter of online browsing to a specific person.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the mechanics of predictive analytics as described in the chapter: retailers merge first-party transaction history with purchased demographics and third-party observation into a Guest ID portrait. Duhigg shows Target used this 'guest portrait' to guess what each household habitually buys and then mailed personalized coupons.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Classify each data source by how Target or its partners obtained it.
assets.column_a_label: First-party transaction data (linked to the shopper's Guest ID)
assets.column_b_label: Demographic data bought or gathered from other firms
assets.column_c_label: Observational data from online conversations, photos, or monitoring

rows.label: A shopper redeems a coupon that Target mailed to her house
Rapleaf reports on a shopper's political leanings and charitable giving
InfiniGraph 'listens' to message-board conversations that mention products favorably
A customer uses her Target-issued credit card at checkout
A company catalogs whether people in posted photos look obese or skinny, tall or short
An estimate of how much money a shopper earns, bought from a data vendor
A shopper fills out a survey and mails in a refund request

distractors: Target cannot link any of its sales to a specific person without a loyalty card.
All of Target's customer data comes from what customers voluntarily reveal on surveys.
Target only collects information through its own stores and never buys data from other firms.
assets.explanation: The focal row sorts to column a because every purchase a customer makes with a Target-issued credit card, frequent-buyer tag, or mailed coupon is recorded and linked to that shopper's Guest ID number in Target's data warehouse. Third-party vendors such as Rapleaf and InfiniGraph supply demographic or conversational data (columns b and c), which Target can also attach to the Guest ID. Andrew Pole reported the system could link about half of all in-store sales, almost all online sales, and about a quarter of online browsing to a specific person.

assets.topic: Sandwiching and camouflage across domains
assets.visual_frame_description: Three side-by-side scenes show the same strategy in different costumes: a radio waveform with a new song slotted between two sticky hits, a direct-mail flyer with a lawnmower ad pressed against a diaper coupon, and a kitchen counter where raw liver disappears into a meatloaf pan. Scenario cards must be dropped into the matching scene.
assets.player_mission: Read each tactic card and assign it to the domain where the book shows it being used to dress something new in old habits: radio, retail mail, or food.
key_concepts: Target mixed ads for things pregnant women would never buy into mailers so the baby ads looked random.
Target placed a coupon for wineglasses next to infant clothes so the products appeared chosen by chance.
A Target executive said that as long as a pregnant woman thinks she hasn't been spied on, she'll use the coupons.
Radio consultant Tom Webster called playing a new song between two consensus popular hits 'textbook playlist theory now.'
WIOQ sandwiched 'Hey Ya!' between sticky hits such as Blu Cantrell's 'Breathe' and 3 Doors Down's 'Here Without You.'
The World War II-era Committee on Food Habits concluded the exotic must be made familiar by camouflaging it in everyday garb.
Soldiers ate chopped and boiled cabbage once it was prepared to look like every other vegetable on their tray.
Butchers handed out recipes explaining how to slip liver into meatloaf.
The chapter's central lesson is that if you dress a new something in old habits, it's easier for the public to accept it.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the camouflage principle: the unfamiliar is accepted when it is dressed in familiar routines, whether a new song between sticky hits, baby coupons beside lawnmower ads, or liver hidden in meatloaf. Duhigg presents the same strategy at work across radio, retail, and wartime food policy.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Sort each tactic into the domain where the book shows it being used to dress something new in old habits.
assets.column_a_label: Radio playlist sandwiching (new song between established hits)
assets.column_b_label: Coupon camouflage (baby ads mixed with unrelated products)

rows.label: WIOQ plays 'Here Without You' by 3 Doors Down right before 'Hey Ya!'
Target puts a lawnmower ad next to a diaper coupon in the same mailer
Butchers hand out recipes that explain how to slip liver into meatloaf
A coupon for wineglasses is placed next to coupons for infant clothes
The Quartermaster Corps chops and boils cabbage until it looks like every other vegetable

Sandwiching only works in radio and has never been applied to retail.
The government's later diet campaigns succeeded by being blunt about health benefits.

The tactic worked because, as one executive put it, as long as a pregnant woman thinks she hasn't been spied on, she'll use the coupons. The radio rows (column a) reflect Tom Webster's 'textbook playlist theory' of playing new songs between consensus hits, and the food rows (column c) reflect the World War II Committee on Food Habits' finding that the exotic must be camouflaged in everyday garb.

assets.topic: Why habits overpower shopping intentions
assets.visual_frame_description: A grocery store aisle is rendered as a decision flowchart. A shopper's handwritten list sits crumpled at the end of the aisle while a product on the shelf triggers a branching decision. Three columns compare point-of-sale habits, store-layout psychology, and individualized Guest ID prediction.
assets.player_mission: Classify each claim by the mechanism the book uses to explain shoppers' behavior. Weigh whether the behavior is a habit firing at the shelf, a layout trick applied to everyone, or a personalized prediction.
key_concepts: Researchers tape-recorded consumers walking through grocery stores to observe how buying decisions were made.
More than 50 percent of purchasing decisions occurred at the moment a customer saw a product on the shelf.
A shopper with a list muttered he would skip the chips, then grabbed the Lay's potato chips when he saw they were on sale.
One woman said of Folgers: 'I'm not crazy about Folgers, but it's what I buy, you know? What else is there?'
Shoppers bought roughly the same amount of food each trip even after pledging to cut back.
Positioning produce at the front gives shoppers a burst of subconscious virtuousness that makes it easier to buy Doritos, Oreos, and frozen pizza later.
Shoppers almost always turn right after entering a store, so retailers stock the right side with the most profitable products.
Cereal and soups shelved out of alphabetical order make shoppers linger and look at a wider selection.
USC psychologists wrote in 2009 that consumers 'automatically repeat past behavior with little regard to current goals.'
Target tried to market to each shopper one by one with personalized pitches designed to appeal to unique buying preferences.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario discriminates among the chapter's three explanations for shopping behavior: habits that fire at the point of sale and override written intentions, one-size-fits-all store-layout psychology, and individualized prediction from Guest ID data. Duhigg reports that more than 50 percent of purchase decisions happen at the shelf because habits are stronger than intentions.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

Produce is placed at the front so a burst of virtuousness makes it easier to buy junk food later

Store-layout tricks such as produce at the front, right-side stocking, and randomized cereal shelves (column b) are the 'primitive, one-size-fits-all' tactics the book contrasts with Target's individualized Guest ID predictions (column c).

assets.topic: Building the pregnancy-prediction algorithm
assets.visual_frame_description: Andrew Pole sits in Target's data lab before a wall of screens showing the baby shower registry, each registrant's due date linked to a Guest ID. A timeline of pregnancy trimesters glows alongside clusters of product icons, and a score dial labeled 'Pregnancy Prediction' sits at the center of the battle interface.
assets.player_mission: Reconstruct Pole's two key moves: identify the earliest purchase signal of a second-trimester pregnancy, then protect the campaign by flagging the shopper most likely to be a false positive before coupons go out.
key_concepts: Pregnant women and new parents are the holy grail of retail because they are among the most profitable, product-hungry, price-insensitive shoppers.
Exhausted new parents buy everything from juice to socks wherever they purchase bottles and formula, and keep coming back for years.
Target's baby shower registry acted as a laboratory because registrants voluntarily handed over their due dates.
Pole identified about twenty-five different products that, analyzed together, let the computer estimate a woman's trimester and due date.
Buying large quantities of unscented lotion around the beginning of the second trimester was a signal picked up from registry data.
Many pregnant women loaded up on vitamins such as calcium, magnesium, and zinc within the first twenty weeks.
Suddenly buying scent-free soap, cotton balls, hand sanitizers, and an astounding number of washcloths suggested the delivery date was near.
Jenny Ward of Atlanta had an 87 percent chance of pregnancy and a late-August due date based on her purchases.
Liz Alter of Brooklyn was given a 96 percent chance of pregnancy and an early-May due date.
A woman who bought only a $250 stroller was probably buying for a friend's baby shower, not pregnant herself.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the mechanics of predictive analytics in the chapter: by combining roughly twenty-five correlated purchase signals with demographic data, Target could score each shopper's likelihood of pregnancy and estimate her due date. Duhigg emphasizes that the model identified patterns from the baby registry and then applied them to every shopper in Target's database.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Target's pregnancy predictor: Andrew Pole combined about twenty-five purchase signals and demographic data into a 'pregnancy prediction' score that estimated whether a shopper was pregnant, what trimester she was in, and her due date, so coupons could be timed to when her habits were most flexible.
assets.stage_1_observation: Andrew Pole pores over the baby shower registry, which acts as a laboratory. Each registrant volunteered her name, her spouse's name, and her due date, letting Pole link the family's Guest IDs and plot every purchase against the trimester in which it occurred. He is searching for the earliest reliable signal of a new pregnancy.
assets.stage_1_question: Which purchase pattern did the registry analysis reveal as a signal that a woman was in the beginning of her second trimester?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Buying unusually large quantities of unscented lotion, along with loading up on vitamins such as calcium, magnesium, and zinc sometime within the first twenty weeks.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The model now scores hundreds of thousands of shoppers, and the marketing team wants to send coupons to the highest-scoring names. You must flag the shopper who is most likely a false positive before her coupons go into the mail.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Flag Caitlin Pike, the thirty-nine-year-old who bought a $250 stroller but nothing else, because she is probably buying for a friend's baby shower and her demographic data shows she was divorced two years ago.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: Turning 'Hey Ya!' from flop into hit
assets.visual_frame_description: A radio control room in 2003 shows the WIOQ playlist scrolling on a screen while an Arbitron graph displays a steep red drop in listeners during the first thirty seconds of 'Hey Ya!'. A hit-prediction dashboard flashes the song's near-record Hit Song Science score, and the tune-out dial sits at 26.6 percent.
assets.player_mission: Diagnose why listeners are rejecting a song the algorithm predicted would be a monster hit, then choose the playlist move that turns the tune-out factor into single digits.
key_concepts: Arista's Steve Bartels was certain 'Hey Ya!' would be huge, and that certainty was not based solely on intuition.
Hit Song Science, built by Polyphonic HMI, analyzed tempo, pitch, melody, and chord progression to predict a song's popularity.
The program predicted Norah Jones's 'Come Away With Me' would be a hit after the industry dismissed it; it sold ten million copies and won eight Grammys.
It also predicted Santana's 'Why Don't You and I' would be popular despite DJs' doubts, and it reached number three on the Billboard Top 40.
'Hey Ya!' received one of the highest Hit Song Science scores anyone had ever seen.
On September 4, 2003, WIOQ played 'Hey Ya!' in the prominent 7:15 p.m. slot, airing it thirty-seven times that month.
Arbitron was testing technology that counted listeners and channel-switching during specific songs, and WIOQ was part of the test.
Nearly a third of listeners changed stations within the first thirty seconds of 'Hey Ya!', and the pattern repeated in Chicago, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Seattle.
Host John Garabedian said Top 40 listeners are offended when something different comes on and don't want anything unfamiliar.
Once 'Hey Ya!' became familiar, a 'Hey Ya!' habit emerged and the song won a Grammy and sold more than 5.5 million albums.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the familiarity principle: even a song with a near-record algorithm score failed until DJs embedded it in existing listening habits. assets.topic: The wartime organ meat campaign
assets.visual_frame_description: A 1940s home kitchen and a military mess hall appear side by side. key_concepts: In the early 1940s the government shipped much of the nation's meat supply to troops, shrinking the availability of steaks and pork chops at home.
The Department of Defense assigned the Committee on Food Habits to figure out how to get Americans to eat organ meats.
More than two hundred studies were eventually published, and at their core was the finding that to change diets, the exotic must be made familiar.
Housewives had to make organ meats look, taste, and smell as similar as possible to what their families expected on the dinner table.
In 1943, soldiers rejected fresh cabbage until mess halls chopped and boiled it to look like every other vegetable.
A present-day researcher wrote that soldiers were more likely to eat food, familiar or not, when it was prepared similar to their prior experiences.
Mailers told housewives that 'every husband will cheer for steak and kidney pie.'
Offal consumption rose by 33 percent during the war and was up 50 percent by 1955.
By 1955, kidney was a staple at dinner, liver was for special occasions, and organ meats had become emblems of comfort.
Later campaigns such as 'Five a Day,' the USDA food pyramid, and the push for low-fat cheeses all failed because none camouflaged their recommendations in existing habits.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the make-the-exotic-familiar principle from the chapter's wartime case: organ meats were accepted only after being camouflaged in everyday dishes. Duhigg contrasts the 1940s success, which raised offal consumption by 33 percent during the war and 50 percent by 1955, with later diet campaigns that failed because they did not camouflage their recommendations.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The Committee on Food Habits' wartime challenge: to change a nation's diet, the exotic must be made familiar. Duhigg argues the 1940s organ meat push was the only government program ever to cause a lasting change in the American diet because it camouflaged new foods in everyday garb.
assets.stage_1_observation: During World War II the Department of Defense recruited sociologists, psychologists, and anthropologists, including Margaret Mead and Kurt Lewin, into the Committee on Food Habits. More than two hundred studies later, the committee concluded that housewives would serve kidneys and livers only if the foods looked, tasted, and smelled like what their families already expected at dinner. Meanwhile, in 1943, soldiers are rejecting the fresh cabbage the Quartermaster Corps begins serving.
assets.stage_1_question: Why did the troops refuse the fresh cabbage, and what made them eat it without complaint?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The cabbage was unfamiliar to their prior experience, so mess halls chopped and boiled it until it looked like every other vegetable on a soldier's tray, after which the troops ate it without complaint.
assets.stage_2_intervention: You are designing the national campaign to sell organ meat to 1940s housewives. Which approach matches what the committee's studies actually found?
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Camouflage the meat in everyday garb: send mailers saying 'every husband will cheer for steak and kidney pie' and give butchers recipes for slipping liver into meatloaf, rather than asking housewives to serve something exotic and unfamiliar.

assets.topic: The YMCA retention insight

assets.player_mission: Analyze the survey data to discover what really keeps YMCA members coming back, then decide where a branch with a limited budget should invest to lift retention.
key_concepts: The YMCA hired a social scientist, Bill Lazarus, and a mathematician, Dean Abbott, to make its branches more competitive.
The two men analyzed data from more than 150,000 YMCA member satisfaction surveys.
YMCA executives believed people wanted fancy exercise equipment and sparkling, modern facilities.
The surveys showed facility attractiveness and machines might cause people to join in the first place.
Retention was driven by emotional factors, such as whether employees knew members' names or said hello when they walked in.
People often go to the gym looking for a human connection, not a treadmill.
A member who made a friend at the YMCA was much more likely to show up for workout sessions.
Lazarus said people want to visit places that satisfy their social needs, and exercising in groups makes it more likely they'll stick with a workout.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: Data-driven retention: the YMCA's accepted wisdom was that fancy equipment keeps members, but analysis of more than 150,000 surveys showed retention was driven by emotional factors and social habits, such as employees knowing members' names and members making friends. The lesson is to wrap a new habit like exercise in an existing one like social connection.

assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Train employees to remember and use members' names and build social connection through group exercise, because a member who makes a friend at the YMCA is much more likely to show up for workouts.

A man in Minnesota stormed into a Target clutching a mailer of baby coupons sent to his high-school daughter.
The manager apologized, and days later the father admitted his daughter was pregnant and due in August.
Target decided to conduct small experiments with specially designed mailers before rolling out a national campaign.
One Target executive described sending customers an ad booklet with everything they bought last week and a coupon for it.
Target mixed in ads for things pregnant women would never buy so the baby ads looked random.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The transparency dilemma: knowing something is not enough, because hiding what you know is sometimes as important as knowing it. Even while following privacy laws, a company can do things that make people queasy, so Target had to deliver pregnancy coupons without making women feel spied on.

assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The algorithm had been right: the daughter was pregnant and due in August, but the mailer revealed knowledge the family had never shared, which is exactly why even legally compliant targeting can make people uncomfortable.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The marketing department wants to roll out the pregnancy campaign nationally. You must choose the rollout strategy that captures the new-parent market without spooking customers.

assets.topic: Andrew Pole weighs the pregnancy-prediction request
assets.visual_frame_description: A Target office in 2002: two marketing colleagues lean over Andrew Pole's cubicle wall while a wall screen behind him streams purchase records tied to Guest ID numbers. The dialogue panel frames each speaker with a small avatar as the player chooses how the statistician responds to the pregnancy-prediction question.
assets.player_mission: Play Andrew Pole and respond to your marketing colleagues' request to identify pregnant customers. Choose the response that reflects how the real project succeeded: cautious, pattern-based, and discreet.
key_concepts: Pregnant women and new parents are the holy grail of retail because they are among the most profitable, product-hungry, price-insensitive shoppers.
If a new parent starts shopping at Target for diapers, they will start buying everything else there as well.
Only a fraction of Target's pregnant customers used the baby shower registry, so the algorithm had to infer pregnancy from purchase patterns.
The baby shower registry acted as a laboratory because registrants handed over their due dates.
Pole identified about twenty-five products that, analyzed together, estimated a woman's trimester and due date.
Pole said he was 'very conservative about compliance with all privacy laws,' but that even following the law, 'you can do things where people get queasy.'
Target ran small experiments with specially designed mailers before launching a national campaign.
An executive said that as long as a pregnant woman thinks she hasn't been spied on, she'll use the coupons.
The chapter's lesson is that hiding what you know is sometimes as important as knowing it.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests predictive pattern analysis of purchase habits combined with the discretion principle: Target succeeded by inferring pregnancy from a bundle of correlated products and by hiding what it knew. Duhigg shows the project only worked once the company tested small mailers and camouflaged the baby ads.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: It is 2002, and you are Andrew Pole, a statistician in Target's Guest Data and Analytical Services department. A few marketing colleagues stop by your desk and ask whether your computers can figure out which customers are pregnant even if they don't want Target to know. Pregnant women are the holy grail of retail, because new parents who start buying diapers at Target tend to buy everything else there too, but identifying them carries a real risk of a privacy backlash. How you respond shapes how the project begins.
dialogue: Marcus (marketing): 'Andrew, quick question. Can your computers figure out which of our customers are pregnant, even the ones who don't want us to know?'
You (Pole): 'Probably. If I can link their purchase history to a Guest ID, I can look for patterns. What would we do with that information?'
Priya (marketing): 'Coupons. Diapers, wipes, nursery furniture. If we catch them in the second trimester, we own their shopping list for years.'
You: 'The registry already tells us when some women are due. The hard part is the women who never register.'
Marcus: 'So it's possible. Great. Let's start mailing baby ads to every woman who buys lotion.'
You: 'Hold on. Lotion alone tells us nothing, because everyone buys lotion. And if we make it obvious we know, women will get queasy. Even following the law, we can cross a line.'
Priya: 'Then what do you suggest?'
You: 'I'll use the registry as a lab, find the products that shift together by trimester, and test small mailers before any national rollout.'
choices: I can build a prediction score from a bundle of products and test it on small groups first, so we don't spook anyone. Hiding what we know matters as much as knowing it.
Let's go big right away. Mail baby coupons to every woman who buys lotion or vitamins; speed matters more than caution.
This is too invasive. I won't use purchase data to infer anyone's pregnancy, no matter what it's worth.
Let's just buy the baby shower registry list and mail only to those women. It's the only legitimate source.
assets.theoretical_principle: Predictive pattern analysis of purchase habits combined with the discretion principle that hiding what you know is as important as knowing it
assets.psychological_breakdown: The optimal response mirrors what Pole actually did: treat the registry as a laboratory, identify roughly twenty-five products that shift together by trimester, and test small mailers before a national rollout. It recognizes that a single product like lotion produces false positives and that even lawful targeting can make customers queasy. Choice 1 ignores both the false-positive problem and the privacy risk, which is exactly the backlash the Minnesota mailer later caused. Choice 2 forgoes a legitimate and enormously profitable analysis. Choice 3 is too narrow because only a fraction of pregnant customers use the registry, leaving the most valuable prospects unreachable.

Top 40 listeners want to hear their favorite songs or songs that sound just like their favorite songs.
Our brains are designed to prefer auditory patterns that seem similar to what we've already heard.
Hit Song Science gave 'Hey Ya!' one of the highest scores anyone had ever seen, yet the song was flailing.
DJs made 'Hey Ya!' familiar by sandwiching it between sticky hits such as Blu Cantrell, 3 Doors Down, and Maroon 5.
Tom Webster called playing a new song between two consensus popular hits 'textbook playlist theory now.'

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.scenario_setup: It is September 2003. You are the music director at WIOQ in Philadelphia. OutKast's 'Hey Ya!' scored among the highest ever on Hit Song Science, but Arbitron's new measurement technology shows nearly a third of listeners change stations within thirty seconds of the song. Arista's Steve Bartels is on the phone urging you to keep it in rotation while your ratings data says listeners are fleeing. Your decision decides whether the song becomes a hit or a flop at your station.
dialogue: Nadia (program director): 'Look at these numbers. Nearly thirty percent of our audience is gone within the first thirty seconds. We can't afford that in drive time.'
You (music director): 'Hit Song Science says this is the biggest hit of the year. The song isn't bad, it's unfamiliar.'
Nadia: 'Unfamiliar equals dead in this format. Top 40 listeners want songs that sound just like their favorite songs.'
You: 'Right. So we don't stop playing it. We change what surrounds it. Rich Meyer's data shows which songs are sticky: Blu Cantrell, 3 Doors Down, Maroon 5. Nobody tunes out on those.'
Nadia: 'You want to bury "Hey Ya!" between them? That feels like hiding the single we're supposed to be promoting.'
You: 'It's playlist theory, risk mitigation. We give listeners a familiar anchor on both sides until the song itself becomes familiar.'
Nadia: 'And how long does that take?'
You: 'If we keep at it, the tune-out factor should keep dropping. By December it could be under six percent.'
choices: Keep it in rotation, but sandwich it between sticky hits like Blu Cantrell and 3 Doors Down so it rides the familiarity of the songs around it.
Pull it from the playlist immediately. The listening data is final and listeners have spoken.
Ignore the tune-out data and double our plays. Hit Song Science gave it the highest score ever, so it will catch on eventually.
Move it to overnight hours where fewer people listen so it can't hurt our ratings.
assets.theoretical_principle: The familiarity principle and playlist sandwiching: embedding a novel song in established listening habits to manage risk
assets.psychological_breakdown: The optimal choice is what WIOQ actually did: it sandwiched 'Hey Ya!' between sticky, familiar hits, dropping the tune-out factor from 26.6 percent in September to 13.7 percent in October and 5.7 percent by December. It works because brains crave familiar auditory patterns, so the novel song borrows familiarity from its neighbors until a 'Hey Ya!' habit emerges. Choice 1 wastes a song the industry needed and that repeated exposure eventually made a Grammy-winning, 5.5-million-album hit. Choice 2 repeats the mistake that caused the initial flop by ignoring how listeners actually react. Choice 3 concedes the song will never work and hides the problem instead of solving it.

assets.domain: Habit Loops | Behavioral Friction & Choice Architecture
assets.topic: The three-part social-habit formula of movements
assets.visual_frame_description: A classroom-style sorting board fills the screen. Three labeled columns stand side by side, and a stack of evidence cards about Rosa Parks's arrest and Rick Warren's church sits beside them. As the player drags each card into a column, the card snaps into place and reveals whether the label is a strong-tie friendship habit, a weak-tie community pressure, or a new habit that builds identity. The setting shifts between a 1955 Montgomery print shop and a modern Orange County living room.
assets.player_mission: Sort each evidence card into exactly one of the three columns of the movement formula from the book. Read the evidence carefully and decide which of the three mechanisms is driving the behavior described, then confirm your classification of the focal card about the newspaper headline.
key_concepts: A movement starts because of the social habits of friendship and the strong ties between close acquaintances.
A movement grows because of the habits of a community and the weak ties that hold neighborhoods and clans together.
A movement endures because leaders give participants new habits that create a fresh sense of identity and a feeling of ownership.
Usually only when all three parts of the process are fulfilled can a movement become self-propelling and reach a critical mass.
Social habits are behaviors that occur unthinkingly across dozens, hundreds, or thousands of people and can fill streets with protesters.
Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955, and her friends across dozens of Montgomery networks responded within hours.
The Advertiser ran an article implying that every black citizen would join the boycott, which made residents assume everyone else was already on board.
Jo Ann Robinson distributed mimeographed flyers through schoolteachers to parents and coworkers within twenty-four hours.
Rick Warren assigned every Saddleback member to a weekly small group so participation became a habit drawing on existing social urges.
Saddleback members sign a maturity covenant card promising daily quiet time, tithing 10 percent of income, and small-group membership.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the three-part mechanism behind social movements: movements ignite through strong-tie friendship habits, spread through weak-tie community expectations, and endure when leaders install new habits that reshape identity. Duhigg presents this as the recurring recipe that turned Rosa Parks's arrest into the Montgomery bus boycott and scaled Rick Warren's Saddleback Church.

credibility.basis: Popular-science journalism with research synthesis (habit loops, keystone habits); some claims simplified.

assets.question: Which column does the Advertiser's 'every black citizen is expected to join Monday's boycott' headline belong to, given that only Parks's friends, the ministers, and the organizers had actually committed at the time?
assets.column_b_label: Weak ties (community expectations and peer pressure)
assets.column_c_label: New habits that build self-identity and ownership

rows.label: E. D. Nixon phones King's closest friend, Ralph Abernathy, to help persuade the hesitant young minister to join the boycott.
The Advertiser publishes that 'every black citizen' will join Monday's boycott, so residents assume everyone else is already on board.
Saddleback asks every member to sign a maturity covenant card promising daily quiet time, tithing, and small-group membership.
Jo Ann Robinson's teachers distribute mimeographed flyers through parents and coworkers across the city.
After the bombing of his house, King gives crowds the habit of answering violence with nonviolence and forgiveness.
Parks's friends in the NAACP, churches, and volunteer circles post bail and agree to show their support.

distractors: Column a, because newspapers are passed around within tight friendship circles.
Column c, because reading a headline permanently changes a person's self-concept.
Column a, because the headline only mattered to the organizers who printed the flyers.
assets.explanation: The headline sorts to column b: when residents read that 'every black citizen' would participate, they assumed the community was already committed and feared that being seen on a bus Monday would look bad. That is exactly the authority of communal expectations and peer pressure that spreads through weak ties, which Duhigg describes as the second part of the movement formula.
